title: Edit Mode vs. Play Mode
content:
# Edit Mode vs. Play Mode

Pixo Builder has two modes. Understanding the difference prevents the most common source
of unexpected scene behavior.

---

## Edit Mode

Edit mode is the default state when you open a Book. In edit mode:

- Behaviors are not active. Wiring in the Behaviors tab exists but does not execute.
- Trait values in the Traits Panel represent the true saved state of your scene.
- Changes you make to traits are permanent until you change them back.

This is where you build and configure. What you see in the Traits Panel is what a learner
will see when the Chapter loads.

## Play Mode

Play mode simulates the learner experience. To enter play mode, click the **play button
(triangle icon)** in the bottom-right corner of the Map Explorer viewport. The button turns
purple when play mode is active.

In play mode:

- All wired behaviors are active and respond to interaction.
- Trait changes that occur as a result of behaviors executing are not saved.
- When you stop play mode, your scene resets to its edit mode state automatically.

Play mode is non-destructive. Testing does not change your scene.

---

## What Chapter Started Is For

"Chapter Started" is a Cause that fires once when a Chapter loads, before the learner
interacts with anything. Anything wired to it runs as part of scene setup.

Because play mode is non-destructive, your scene already returns to its edit mode state
when you stop testing. You do not need Chapter Started to reset your scene.

Use Chapter Started when you want specific behaviors to execute at the moment the Chapter
loads — setting a State Machine to a known starting state, triggering an audio cue, making
an object visible or hidden, or any other action that needs to run before the learner
touches anything. It runs initialization behaviors, not just trait assignment.

It is also useful as an explicit redundancy. If there is something in your scene where you
want to guarantee the starting state rather than rely on your edit mode values, wire it to
Chapter Started. That makes the starting condition an authored behavior, visible in the
behavior tree, rather than something implicit.

---

## Common Scenario

You are testing a scene. You interact with an object and it moves. You exit play mode.
The object is back where it was.

That is expected behavior. Play mode is non-destructive — edit mode state is preserved.

If you want to ensure that object starts at a specific position every time a learner loads
the Chapter — regardless of anything else — wire a Chapter Started Cause to a Move Effect
and set the position explicitly. Now the starting position is an authored behavior, not
an assumption.

---

## Summary

| | Edit Mode | Play Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviors active | No | Yes |
| Trait changes saved | Yes | No |
| Use for | Building and configuring | Testing and validating |

title: Building a UI Panel
content:
# Building a UI Panel

This walkthrough takes you from an empty scene to a functioning UI panel. By the end, you will have a Billboard in the scene with Symbol Sparks placed on it and at least one interactive behavior wired.

---

## Step 1 — Add a Billboard

Open the **Spark Browser** and navigate to **Symbols / UI Containers**. You will find two Billboard types:

**Billboard** — placed at a fixed position in world space. The learner must be facing it to see it. Use this for instructional panels, tool descriptions, or any UI anchored to a specific location in the environment.

**Follow Head Billboard** — follows the learner's view and is always visible regardless of where they look or move. Use this for persistent heads-up display elements: progress indicators, instructions that must always be readable, or overlays that need to stay in frame.

Drag the Billboard type you want into the scene from the Spark Browser or drop it directly into the Map Explorer.

> **Rename the Instance immediately.** If your scene has more than one Billboard, default names become confusing fast. Set a descriptive Instance Name in the Traits Panel as soon as the Billboard is placed. You will be selecting it by name from a dropdown in the UI Editor.

---

## Step 2 — Configure the Billboard

With the Billboard Instance selected, the **Traits Panel** shows its configuration options. Set these before you start adding content:

**Canvas Resolution (X, Y)** — sets the pixel dimensions of the Billboard's canvas. This controls the resolution of the 2D surface, not the physical size of the object in the scene. The default is 1920 × 1080. Adjust physical size using Scale or the Gizmo.

**Background Color** — sets the background color of the canvas. Use the RGBA values to set color and transparency.

**Rotate towards camera** — when enabled, the Billboard automatically rotates so its front face always points at the player's camera, regardless of where the player is standing. Useful for world-anchored panels that should always be readable.

**Lock X Auto-Rotate / Lock Y Auto-Rotate** — constrains the auto-rotation axis when Rotate towards camera is enabled. Locking X is the most common setting: the Billboard rotates horizontally to face the player, but does not tilt up or down. Locking Y allows tilt but prevents horizontal rotation.

**Rotation** — if Rotate towards camera is disabled, set the Billboard's orientation manually. Billboards only display content on one face, and an empty canvas gives no visual indication of which side is the front.

> **Note:** An empty Billboard looks identical from both sides. If you rotate it now and get the direction wrong, it is easy to miss. Consider adding a Symbol Spark first (Step 4), which makes the front face immediately visible, then adjusting rotation.

---

## Step 3 — Open the UI Editor

Click the **UI Editor** tab in the top navigation bar.

In the **upper right of the UI Editor panel**, a dropdown lists every Billboard Instance in the current Chapter. Select the Billboard you just placed. The canvas for that Billboard appears in the workspace.

> **Note:** If the Billboard's visibility is set to hidden in the scene, the UI Editor canvas will appear blank — content is invisible and cannot be interacted with. This is a known issue. To work around it, use the **Is Visible** toggle in the upper left of the UI Editor panel (this is a shortcut to set the Billboard's visibility trait to true). Make your edits, then re-hide the Billboard when you are done if it should be hidden at Chapter start.

---

## Step 4 — Add Symbol Sparks

With your Billboard selected in the UI Editor dropdown, the **Spark Browser** displays the Symbol Sparks library. Symbol Sparks are organized into subfolders: Interactive (buttons, toggles, input fields), Primitives (shapes), and others.

**To add a Symbol Spark:** drag it from the Spark Browser directly onto the Billboard canvas in the UI Editor.

Once placed, you can:

- **Move** — drag the element to reposition it on the canvas
- **Resize** — drag the handles to scale the element
- **Nudge precisely** — use the **arrow keys** to move a selected Symbol Spark in small increments
- **Edit traits** — select the element and adjust its properties in the Traits Panel (text content, colors, font size, and more)

The **Sort Order** trait controls which Symbol Spark appears in front when elements overlap — higher values render on top. This matters if you have overlapping UI elements where one should stay clickable.

**Image backgrounds:** To use an image as a background or decorative element, import the image as an **ImageViewer Spark** and place it on the canvas the same way as any other Symbol Spark. See [Importing Assets](../importing-assets.md) for import instructions. [PENDING: Importing Assets guide not yet written — link when available.]

---

## Step 5 — Wire Behaviors

Switch to the **Behaviors tab** to wire interactive logic for the Symbol Sparks on your Billboard.

Layout is handled in the UI Editor. Interactivity is handled in the Behaviors tab. To make a UI element do something, you must wire it in the Behaviors tab.

**Example — a button that changes Chapter:**

1. In the Behaviors tab, use the Instance dropdown to select your Button Instance.
2. Add an **On Button Pressed** Cause.
3. Add a **Change Chapter** Effect on the Chapter Config Spark Instance.
4. Wire the output of On Button Pressed to the input of Change Chapter.

Entering a chapter name or index in the Change Chapter Effect parameters determines where the learner is taken when the button is pressed.

For Causes, Effects, and parameters specific to each Symbol Spark type, see the [Symbol Sparks Reference](../symbol-sparks/README.md).

---

## What you just built

A Billboard defines a canvas in the scene — either fixed in world space or following the learner's head. Symbol Sparks are the content elements on that canvas. Behaviors connect the two to scene logic. These three pieces always work together: container, content, and behavior.

From here, the same pattern applies to any UI you build: add a Billboard, populate it with Symbol Sparks, wire the interactions you need.

title: Creating UI Panels
content:
# Creating UI Panels

A UI panel in Pixo Builder is a flat, 2D interface embedded in the 3D scene — a screen the learner can see, read, and interact with during a session. UI panels display text, buttons, images, and other interactive elements.

Building a UI panel in Builder requires two components working together:

**Billboard** — an Entity Spark that acts as the container for the UI. The Billboard defines where the panel exists in the scene, how large it is, and how it faces the player. It has no content of its own; it is the canvas.

**Symbol Sparks** — the 2D elements placed inside the Billboard. These are the visible, interactive pieces: buttons, text labels, images, dropdowns, toggles, and more.

A Billboard without Symbol Sparks is an empty canvas. Symbol Sparks cannot exist in the scene without a Billboard to contain them. You always need both.

---

## In This Section

- [Building a UI Panel](building-a-ui-panel.md) — Step-by-step walkthrough from empty scene to a working interactive UI panel, including how to add a Billboard, configure it, place Symbol Sparks, and wire behaviors.

title: Core Concepts
content:
# Core Concepts

Before you start building, there are four concepts that underpin everything else in Builder. A solid understanding of these will provide a strong foundation for learning the rest of the tool.

---

## Books and Chapters

A **Book** is a Builder project. It is saved as a single file and contains everything that makes up one training experience — the scenes, the objects, the behaviors, the logic.

A **Chapter** is a self-contained scene inside a Book. A Book always has at least one Chapter. Most training experiences contain several — for example, one Chapter per scenario, or one Chapter for a main menu and additional Chapters for each module.

Each Chapter has its own set of objects, its own 3D environment, and its own behavior logic. Moving between Chapters is how learners navigate between scenes in the final experience.

---

## Sparks and Spark Instances

This is the most important concept in Builder, and the one that most commonly trips up new users.

A **Spark** is a template — a reusable definition. Think of it as the source definition for an object. It lives in the Spark Browser. You do not interact with a Spark directly in a scene; you use it to create copies.

A **Spark Instance** is a placed copy of a Spark in the scene. When you drag a Spark from the Spark Browser into the scene, you create a Spark Instance. That Instance is the thing you can move, configure, and wire behaviors to.

**Why this matters:** You can place the same Spark multiple times to create multiple Instances — a fire extinguisher placed in five locations, for example. Each Instance is independent. Behaviors you add to one Instance do not automatically apply to the others.

You will always be working with Spark Instances, not Sparks directly.

### Spark types

All Sparks fall into three types:

**Entity Sparks** are 3D objects — physical things that exist in space in the scene. Most of what you place in a scene will be Entity Sparks. Entity Sparks have a 3D model and can be positioned, rotated, and scaled. "Environment Sparks" are a specialized Entity Spark subtype that define invisible spatial zones, useful for detecting when a learner has moved into an area.

**Config Sparks** are logic and configuration elements with no 3D presence. They exist in the scene as logic only — things like state trackers and sequence managers. You will not see a Config Spark Instance in the 3D environment, but it participates in behavior logic. "State Machine" and "Datum" are examples of Config Sparks.

**Symbol Sparks** are 2D interface elements — buttons, text, images, and similar components — used to build on-screen UI. Symbol Sparks are placed inside Billboards (specialized 3D surfaces that display 2D content), not directly in 3D space.

---

## Causes, Effects, and Behavior Trees

**Causes** and **Effects** are the two sides of behavior in Builder.

A **Cause** is something that happens — a trigger. An object being interacted with, a timer finishing, a learner entering a zone.

An **Effect** is something that happens as a result. An object highlighting, audio playing, a scene changing, text updating.

You wire Causes to Effects in the Behaviors tab. One Cause can connect to multiple Effects. One Effect can receive connections from multiple Causes. Any Cause can connect to any Effect — there are no compatibility restrictions.

**A simple example:** Wire an "Interacted" Cause to a "Highlight" Effect on a fire extinguisher Instance. When the learner interacts with the extinguisher, it highlights. That is a behavior.

When you wire Causes and Effects together, you are building a **behavior tree** — the interactive logic of a Chapter. A behavior tree can be a single Cause-to-Effect connection, or a complex branching structure with conditional logic and multiple paths. Any Spark Instance in the Chapter can contribute Causes and Effects to the tree. The instance dropdown in the Behaviors tab controls which instance you are adding nodes from. All behaviors in a Chapter share the same canvas.

**A note on Modifiers:** The Behaviors tab has a third row alongside Causes and Effects called Modifiers. These behaviors — "Chapter Started" (fires when a Chapter loads), "Delay" (pauses a chain), "Change Chapter" (moves the learner to another scene) — belong to the Modifier Spark, a built-in Config Spark that is included in every Chapter by default. You do not place it; it is always there. They are covered in the [Wiring Behaviors](../wiring-behaviors/) section.

Start with a single Cause connected to a single Effect. Complexity builds from there.

title: Edit Mode and Play Mode
content:
# Edit Mode and Play Mode

Builder has two modes: Edit mode and Play mode. Understanding the difference between them prevents one of the most common sources of confusion for new users.

---

## Edit mode

Edit mode is the default state when you open a Book. In edit mode:

- Behaviors are **not active** — wiring exists, but nothing fires
- Trait values in the Traits Panel are **stable** and represent the saved starting state of each Instance
- Changes you make are **saved** when you save the Book

This is where you build. Placing Spark Instances, configuring their Traits, and wiring Behaviors in the Behaviors tab all happen in edit mode.

---

## Play mode

Play mode activates the scene. You enter play mode by pressing the play button (the triangle in the bottom-right corner of the Map Explorer). In play mode:

- Behaviors become **active** — Causes fire and Effects execute as designed
- Trait values can change as behavior logic runs (a highlight turns on, an object moves, text updates)
- Those runtime changes are **not saved** — when you stop play mode, the Chapter reloads from its last saved state on disk. Any unsaved edits made in edit mode before entering play mode will also be discarded.

This is where you test. Run your interactions, check that behaviors fire as expected, and experience the scene as a learner would.

**Save before entering play mode.** Stopping play mode reloads the Chapter from disk — any unsaved edits will be discarded.

The play button turns **purple** while play mode is active.

---

## The critical rule: runtime changes do not persist

Builder does not store a separate "initial state" snapshot. The Traits Panel values you set in edit mode *are* the initial state.

This means: if you interact with objects during testing and they move, change state, or update in some way, those changes disappear when you stop play mode. The scene resets every time you enter play mode. This is the correct behavior — it is what makes testing non-destructive.

**However:** if you move a Spark Instance in edit mode and then save, that new position becomes the permanent starting state. There is no undo of a save that recovers a prior position. Set your initial trait values deliberately in edit mode.

---

## What Chapter Started is for

Chapter Started is a Cause that fires once when a Chapter loads, before the learner interacts with anything. Anything wired to it runs as part of scene setup.

Because play mode is non-destructive, your scene already returns to its edit mode state when you stop testing. You do not need Chapter Started to reset your scene.

Use Chapter Started when you want specific behaviors to execute at the moment the Chapter loads — setting a State Machine to a known starting state, triggering an audio cue, making an object visible or hidden, or any other action that needs to run before the learner touches anything. It runs initialization behaviors, not just trait assignment.

It is also useful as an explicit redundancy. If there is something in your scene where you want to guarantee the starting state rather than rely on your edit mode values, wire it to Chapter Started. That makes the starting condition an authored behavior, visible in the behavior tree, rather than something implicit.

---

## Common scenario: objects that move during testing

You are testing a scene. You interact with an object and it moves. You exit play mode. The object is back where it started.

That is expected behavior. Play mode is non-destructive — edit mode state is preserved.

If you want to ensure that object starts at a specific position every time a learner loads the Chapter — regardless of anything else — wire a Chapter Started Cause to a Move Effect and set the position explicitly. Now the starting position is an authored behavior, not an assumption.

---

## Quick reference

| | Edit mode | Play mode |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviors active | No | Yes |
| Trait changes saved | Yes (on save) | No |
| Use for | Building, configuring | Testing, experiencing |
| Play button color | Default | Purple |

title: Overview
content:
# Overview

Pixo Builder is a no-code authoring tool for creating interactive XR training experiences. It runs on your desktop and produces content that plays back on VR headsets, mobile devices, and desktop — through the companion Pixo Player application.

## What you build with Builder

A Builder project is called a Book. Each Book contains one or more Chapters, and each Chapter is a self-contained interactive scene: a 3D environment with objects in it, and logic that defines how those objects behave when learners interact with them.

The core authoring action in Builder is behavior wiring: you define what happens when something occurs. Something happens (a Cause) — you connect it to a consequence (an Effect). That connection is a behavior. String several behaviors together and you have a behavior tree. A Chapter full of behavior trees becomes an interactive training experience.

You do not write code. You make connections.

## Who Builder is for

Builder is designed for instructional designers and training developers who need to produce interactive VR content without relying on a dedicated engineering team. You do not need a background in game development, 3D software, or programming.

If you are comfortable thinking in steps, sequences, and conditional logic — "if the learner does this, then this should happen" — you already think the way Builder is designed to work.

## How Builder fits into the Pixo Platform

Builder is the authoring tool. When you are ready to distribute a training experience, you publish your Book to the Pixo Platform, which handles delivery to learners, device management, and LMS integration. Pixo Player — the application installed on learner devices — pulls published content from the platform and runs it.

You build in Builder. Learners experience it in Pixo Player. The Pixo Platform connects the two.

## What this guide covers

The Getting Started section walks you through the complete setup process and the foundational concepts you need before building your first scene. By the end, you will have Builder installed, an account configured, and enough context to follow the First Success Walkthrough — where you build and test your first working interaction.

title: The Builder Workspace
content:
# The Builder Workspace

When you open a Book, you are looking at the Builder workspace. This page introduces each panel and explains what it is for. You do not need to master any of these panels right now — the goal is to know where things are and what they do before you start using them.

The layout described here is the default. Builder's workspace is fully customizable — panels can be rearranged, resized, or reset to default from the Settings tab in the right panel.

<!-- SCREENSHOT PLACEHOLDER: builder-workspace.png shows Bonfire Builder (pre-rename). Replace with a clean Pixo Builder screenshot before public launch. -->
![The Builder workspace](../../../assets/images/builder-workspace.png)

---

## Left panel

The left panel has four tabs across the top:

- **Help** — in-app tutorial videos and reference content
- **Chapters** — the structure of your Book; navigate between Chapters here
- **Behaviors** — where Causes and Effects get wired together. Select a Spark Instance and switch to this tab to add and connect behaviors. Sparks have no default behavior tree — the canvas will be empty until you wire something up. This is the core authoring workspace in Builder — if you spend time in one place, it will be here.

  The Behaviors tab has three rows for building your logic:
  - **Causes** — select the event that triggers a behavior (dropdown + search + `+` to add)
  - **Effects** — select what happens when the Cause fires (`+` to add)
  - **Modifiers** — scene-level behaviors for initialization, timing, navigation, and debugging; select "Chapter Started", "Delay", "Change Chapter", and others from this dropdown

  At the bottom of the panel are canvas organization tools:
  - **Group / Ungroup** — group selected nodes together to keep the canvas organized
  - **Comment** — add a text annotation to the canvas to label or explain a section of logic
  - **Sub Graph** — collapse a set of connected nodes into a reusable sub-graph
- **Ember** — Builder's scripting layer for advanced logic. You will not need Ember for basic interactions.

---

## Bottom center pane

The bottom center pane sits below the 3D viewport. It has four tabs:

- **Sparks** — your library of all available Sparks (Entity, Config, Symbol, and Environment)
- **Maps** — the environments available to load into a Chapter
- **Presets** — saved Spark configurations you can reuse across Books. A Preset captures one or more Spark Instances and their wired behaviors, including cross-Spark wiring relationships. To create a Preset, select one or more Spark Instances in the scene and click the **+** button (Create Preset from Selected) in the Presets toolbar. Presets are stored in **My Presets** and can be dragged into any Book. Not needed in early sessions.
- **Console** — a log of runtime output with timestamps. Use the filter icons to show only errors or warnings, and the Clear and Collapse buttons to manage the log. As a beginner, the Console is useful for spotting errors or confirming that behaviors fired. If something is not working as expected, checking the Console is a good first step.

---

## Center section: Map Editor, Map Explorer, UI Editor, and Step Manager

The large center area of the workspace is tabbed. Map Editor, Map Explorer, UI Editor, and the soon-to-be-released Step Manager all live here as separate tabs. You switch between them depending on what you are doing.

### Map Editor

The Map Editor is a construction view with a fixed overhead or side-on camera. It is designed for precise placement, positioning, and arrangement of Spark Instances — you can see the scene from above, snap objects to a grid, and position things exactly where you want them.

The Map Editor has several camera orientations: Top Down, Bottom Up, North-South, South-North, East-West, West-East, and Fly Cam (free movement). The top of the panel shows buttons to switch between orientations.

Key tools in the Map Editor:
- **Gizmo** — the transform control that appears when you select a Spark Instance. Drag the colored lines to move along a single axis, the colored squares to move within a plane, the green arc to rotate, or the white center box to scale uniformly. No mode switching required.
- **Snap** — snaps Spark Instances to a grid for precise placement
- **X-Ray Mode** — moves the camera along a selected axis, cutting through Spark Instances in a plane, useful for seeing inside complex scenes
- **Zoom to Player / Zoom to Selected** — camera shortcuts to quickly re-center your view

Use the Map Editor when you are building and arranging your scene.

### Map Explorer

The Map Explorer is the player-perspective view. The camera is attached to a player character in first or third person, and you navigate as a learner would. This is where you test your scene, run behaviors, and experience your content before publishing.

**Navigation controls:**

| Action | Control |
|---|---|
| Move | WASD or Arrow Keys |
| Look around | Right-click + drag mouse |
| Interact with an object | E |
| Grab an object | R |
| Click a UI element | Mouse click |

Controls follow standard Unity conventions.

Key tools in the Map Explorer toolbar:
- **Physics toggle** — turns player physics on or off (useful when you want to fly around the scene during testing)
- **Reload Chapter** — reloads the current Chapter
- **Start Chapter** — launches the full Chapter experience as a learner would experience it, running the complete behavior tree from the beginning
The play button is in the bottom-right corner of the Map Explorer. It turns purple when play mode is active. Stopping play mode always resets all Instance states back to their saved Traits values — see [Edit Mode and Play Mode](edit-mode-and-play-mode.md) for why this matters.

Use the Map Explorer when you are testing interactions, navigating your scene, or experiencing it as a learner would.

### UI Editor

The UI Editor is a dedicated panel for building 2D interface content displayed on a Billboard. When a Billboard Instance is selected, the UI Editor lets you add and arrange Symbol Sparks — buttons, text, images, and other 2D components — on the Billboard's surface.

You do not need the UI Editor in your first session. It becomes relevant when you start building on-screen instructions, step prompts, or menus.

### Step Manager

The Step Manager is an upcoming tab for managing structured step-by-step flows. It is not yet released.

---

## Right side: two distinct panels

The right side of the workspace contains two separate panels: the **right panel** (Traits, Notes, and Settings tabs), which shows properties for the currently selected Spark Instance, and the **Instances pane**, which tracks everything placed in the scene. They serve different purposes and are always both visible.

## Right panel

The right panel has three tabs: Traits, Notes, and Settings.

### Traits

The Traits tab is instance-specific. When you select a Spark Instance, this tab shows its configurable properties: position, scale, visibility, interactability, and other attributes specific to that Spark type. These values are the starting state of the Instance when a Chapter loads.

Behaviors can change trait values at runtime, but those runtime changes do not overwrite the values set here — see [Edit Mode and Play Mode](edit-mode-and-play-mode.md) for why this matters.

### Notes

The Notes tab is book-level. It is a free-text field for documenting your Book — authoring context, reminders, or anything you want to preserve for yourself or collaborators. It is not tied to any specific Instance.

### Settings

The Settings tab is also book-level. It contains layout controls (Open Layout, Save Current Layout, Reset Layout to Default) and workspace preferences including UI Scale, Mouse Sensitivity, and Performance Mode.

---

## Instances pane

On the bottom right of the workspace is the Instances pane, which tracks everything currently placed in your scene. It is organized into three tabs:

- **Entities** — all Entity Spark Instances (3D objects and Environment Sparks)
- **Config** — all Config Spark Instances (logic elements, audio, State Machines, etc.)
- **Symbols** — all Symbol Spark Instances (2D UI elements on Billboards)

Each tab has a Select dropdown at the top for filtering the list. Clicking an Instance in this pane selects it in the scene. This is also the correct way to delete an Instance — right-click it here and choose Remove. Do not delete Sparks from the Spark Browser, which removes the template, not a placed copy. If you delete a Spark from the browser, all Instances of that Spark in your scene are replaced with placeholder primitives.

---

## Keyboard shortcuts

Builder supports standard keyboard shortcuts for common editing actions:

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Cmd+S / Ctrl+S | Save |
| Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z | Undo |
| Cmd+Y / Ctrl+Y | Redo |
| Cmd+C / Ctrl+C | Copy selected node(s) or Instance(s) |
| Cmd+V / Ctrl+V | Paste |
| Cmd+A / Ctrl+A | Select all |
| Arrow Keys | Micro-adjust position of selected element in the UI Editor |

These shortcuts work in the Behaviors tab (for nodes and Subgraphs), the Map Editor, and the UI Editor. Standard OS conventions apply — Cmd on Mac, Ctrl on Windows.

---

## What to open first

When you start a new session in Builder, the recommended sequence is:

1. Open or create a Book
2. Open Map Explorer — get oriented in the scene
3. Open the bottom center pane — find what you want to place
4. Drag a Spark into the scene to create an Instance
5. Select the Instance and open the Behaviors tab to start wiring

You will learn the Map Editor and other panels as you need them.

title: Glossary
content:
# Glossary

Definitions for terms used throughout Pixo Builder documentation.

---

## Writing Conventions

**Named UI elements use quotation marks**

When referring to a named Spark, Cause, Effect, Modifier, panel, or other named Builder element in prose, the proper name appears in quotation marks. This makes multi-word names parse clearly as a single unit.

Example: Datum values can be displayed in the scene using a "Datum Viewer" Symbol Spark.

Applies to: Spark names ("Proximity Trigger"), Cause/Effect/Modifier names ("Chapter Started"), panel names ("Behaviors tab"), and any other named element from the Builder UI. Does not apply to generic type words like Spark, Cause, Effect, Chapter, Book.

---

## Core Concepts

**Book**
The standard term for a project in Pixo Builder. A Book contains one or more Chapters and is saved as a Builder project file. When published, a Book is uploaded to a CDN and can be delivered to any Pixo Player regardless of device. Authors typically work on one Book per training experience.

**Chapter**
A self-contained scene within a Book. Each Chapter has its own map, behavior tree, and set of Spark Instances. A Book always contains at least one Chapter. Authors split content across multiple Chapters when a single scene would exceed memory limits, or when a project calls for selectable scenarios — for example, branching from a main menu.

**Map**
The spatial environment that Spark Instances are placed into. A Map defines the physical space of a scene — floors, walls, and geometry that the player can navigate. Maps are created from GLB/GLTF files and managed in the Maps Browser. A Map is not a Spark — it is the container that Spark Instances inhabit. A Chapter can have one or more Maps.

**Spark**
The fundamental building block of everything in Pixo Builder. A Spark is a template definition — a reusable modular component that can represent objects, logic, environments, configuration, or behavior. Everything in the system is a Spark. Sparks come in three formal types: Entity Sparks, Symbol Sparks, and Config Sparks.

**Entity Spark**
A Spark that contains 3D information — objects, environments, and other elements that exist in physical space in the scene. Entity Sparks are the primary building blocks for constructing scenes. Environment Sparks and Billboards are specialized subtypes of Entity Sparks.

**Environment Spark**
A specialized Entity Spark subtype that defines an invisible spatial zone within a scene. Environment Sparks have no visible 3D model — they exist purely as triggers. Their primary Cause fires when the player enters the zone, making them useful for spatial checkpoints, area-based progression gates, and delivery confirmation steps in training flows.

**Symbol Spark**
A Spark used within a UI Panel. Symbol Sparks are 2D interface elements — buttons, dropdowns, images, 2D primitives, text, and similar components. Where Entity Sparks exist in 3D space, Symbol Sparks exist in flat UI layers.

**Config Spark**
A Spark with no 3D component — logical or configuration elements that affect behavior without having a physical presence in the scene. Audio is grouped with Config Sparks since there is no 3D model associated with it. Config Sparks participate in behavior trees as both Causes and Effects — they can fire events and respond to them. The "State Machine" and "Step Manager" are the most commonly used Config Sparks in training content.

**UI Panel**
A 2D interface layer within a scene, built using Symbol Sparks. UI Panels allow authors to create interactive flat interfaces — menus, instruction screens, buttons, and similar elements — within an otherwise 3D environment. UI Panels are attached to and displayed through Billboards.

**Billboard**
A specialized Entity Spark subtype that serves as a 3D-positioned surface for displaying a UI Panel. A Billboard exists in physical space — it can be placed, scaled, and positioned like any other Entity Spark — but its face displays 2D UI content built from Symbol Sparks in the UI Editor. Billboards are the bridge between the 3D scene and 2D interface elements. Authors typically use Billboards to display on-screen instructions, step prompts, menus, and feedback messages within a training experience.

**Spark Instance**
A placed copy of a Spark in the scene. When a user drags a Spark from the Spark Browser into the Map Editor or Map Explorer, they create a Spark Instance. The Instance inherits from the Spark but can have its own property overrides. See [Core Concepts](getting-started/core-concepts/) for a full explanation of this distinction.

**Behavior**
The umbrella term for the interactive elements in Pixo Builder. Behaviors come in two types: Causes and Effects. Users string behaviors together in the Behaviors tab to create behavior trees that define how Spark Instances respond to events.

**Cause**
One of the two types of Behavior. A Cause is a trigger — something that happens to initiate a behavior tree. Examples: "Interacted", "Timer Elapsed", "Entered Zone". Causes have outputs that connect to Effect inputs.

**Effect**
The second type of Behavior. An Effect is the result of a Cause firing. Examples: "Highlight", "Visible", "Change Chapter". Effects have inputs that receive connections from Cause outputs.

**Behavior Tree**
The result of stringing one or more Causes and Effects together in the Behaviors tab. Behavior trees define the full interactive logic of a Spark Instance. Any Cause can connect to any Effect — universal compatibility is a key product strength.

**Modifier**
A special built-in Spark that is permanently present in every Chapter — authors do not place it and it cannot be removed. Its behaviors appear in the Modifiers row of the Behaviors tab alongside Causes and Effects. Key Modifier behaviors include "Chapter Started" (fires when a Chapter loads), "Delay" (pauses a behavior chain), "Toggle" (alternates signal between two outputs), "Change Chapter", "Exit Book", and "Debug" (sends a message to the Console). In early sessions, "Chapter Started" and "Delay" are the most immediately useful.

**Behavior Wiring**
The act of connecting Cause outputs to Effect inputs visually in the Behaviors tab. This is the core interaction model of Builder.

**State Machine**
A built-in Config Spark that tracks a named state value and gates behavior based on which state is currently active. Authors define a set of named states (for example, "End A" and "End B") and configure a starting state. The State Machine participates in behavior trees from both sides: as an Effect, it acts as a conditional gate — firing its output only if the current state matches a specified value, then updating the state. As a Cause, it fires when a specific state is entered. This makes the State Machine the primary tool for building conditional branching logic in Builder.

**Step Manager**
A built-in Config Spark that tracks a learner's position within a defined sequence of steps and gates advancement through that sequence. Authors configure a numbered list of steps and a starting step. The Step Manager participates in behavior trees from both sides: as an Effect, it acts as a conditional gate — firing its output only if the learner is currently on a specified step, then advancing to the next step. As a Cause, it fires when a specific step is entered. Step Manager is appropriate for compliance training and procedure-based content where sequence matters. It is not appropriate for exploratory or scenario-based content where learners make open-ended choices.

**Sub Graph**
A collapsed grouping of behavior nodes within the Behaviors tab. When a behavior tree grows complex, authors can select a collection of nodes and collapse them into a single Sub Graph block with a label. Sub Graphs are an organizational tool only — they do not change how the behavior logic executes.

---

## UI Panels

**Spark Browser**
Panel for browsing and finding available Sparks, organized in folders. Users drag Sparks from here into the Map Editor or Map Explorer to create Spark Instances.

**Map Editor**
A scene construction view with a fixed camera for precise Spark Instance placement and positioning. Camera orientations include Top Down, Bottom Up, North-South, South-North, East-West, West-East, and Fly Cam. Key tools: Snap (grid alignment), X-Ray Mode (cut-plane visibility), and Zoom to Player / Zoom to Selected.

**Map Explorer**
A player-perspective view for testing and experiencing the scene. The camera is attached to the player character in first or third person. Navigation: WASD or Arrow Keys to move, right-click + drag to look, E to interact, R to grab, mouse click for UI elements. Key tools: Physics toggle, Reload Chapter, Start Chapter.

**Behaviors tab**
Where Causes and Effects are added to a selected Spark Instance and behavior wiring connections are made. The workspace for building behavior trees.

**Traits Panel**
Displays instance-specific properties for a selected Spark Instance — configurable attributes such as position, scale, and visibility that can be overridden per instance.

**UI Editor**
A dedicated panel for building the 2D interface content displayed on a Billboard. When a Billboard Instance is selected and the UI Editor is open, authors can add and arrange Symbol Sparks on the Billboard's surface. The Behaviors tab is still used to wire the interactive logic of those Symbol Sparks.

**Gizmo**
The transform control that appears when a Spark Instance is selected in the Map Editor. Provides color-coded handles for moving, rotating, and scaling instances — no mode switching required.

---

## Product Terms

**Pixo Builder**
The authoring tool. Use this name in all external communications and documentation.

**Pixo Player**
The runtime application used to experience content built in Pixo Builder. Device-specific Player applications are available for Pico, Quest, PC Desktop, Mac OS, iOS, and Android. All Players run the same published Book regardless of device.

**Pixo Platform**
The platform layer that connects Builder (authoring) to Pixo Player (delivery). Handles publishing, LMS integration, device management, and learner analytics. When an author publishes from Builder, the Book is uploaded to the Pixo Platform and made available to Pixo Player.

title: Behavior Wiring Reference
content:
# Behavior Wiring Reference

This reference covers behaviors available across all Spark types in Pixo Builder.

- **Entity Spark Causes and Effects** — see [Entity Spark Behaviors](entity-sparks/entity-spark-behaviors.md)
- **Config Spark behaviors** — documented on individual Config Spark pages
- **Symbol Spark behaviors** — documented on individual Symbol Spark pages
- **Modifier behaviors** — see [Modifiers](modifiers/README.md); available in every Chapter regardless of what else is in the scene

For an overview of how the Behaviors tab works, see [Behaviors tab](ui-panels/behavior-panel.md).

---

## Base Spark Behaviors

Every Spark in Pixo Builder — Entity, Config, and Symbol — inherits three behaviors from the base Spark class:

- **Trait Is…** (Cause) — fires when a specified trait on this Instance meets a defined condition
- **If Trait Is…** (Effect) — conditional gate; passes signal through only if a condition on this Instance is true at the moment it is triggered
- **Modify** (Effect) — sets the value of any exposed trait on this Instance at runtime

These are available on every Spark Instance.

---

## Notes

### No Initial State

Builder does not store a separate "initial state" for Spark Instance traits. If you modify a Spark Instance during testing and save the Book, that modification becomes the new starting state.

**The standard workaround:** use Chapter Started to initialize all critical trait values at the start of each Chapter — positions, visibility states, interactability settings — so the Chapter always starts in a known state.

---

*Pending items require developer confirmation before publishing. Search for `[PENDING` to find all unresolved entries.*

title: Audio
content:
# Audio

*`[PENDING: Audio system is under revision. Documentation below is based on current behavior and may change before trial launch. Verify with developer before publishing.]`*

An Audio Config Spark plays sound effects. Add it to the scene from the Config Sparks browser under the Audio folder. The audio clip is associated with the Spark at authoring time; the "Audio" Effect controls playback at runtime.

Audio Sparks are assigned to named channels (Dialog1–3, Music1–3, SoundFX1–3). Channels can be stopped mid-playback using the "Stop Audio Channel" Modifier.

---

## Effects

### Audio

Controls playback of the audio clip associated with this Spark.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Clip | The audio clip to play |
| State | **Play** — start playback. **Pause** — temporarily halt. **Stop** — halt and reset. |
| Volume | Playback volume — 0 is silent, 1 is full volume |
| Solo | When enabled, stops all other currently playing audio |

### Change Audio Channel Trait

Reassigns this Audio Spark to a different channel at runtime.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| New Channel | Dialog1, Dialog2, Dialog3, Music1, Music2, Music3, SoundFX1, SoundFX2, SoundFX3 |

### Modify

Sets the Loop Audio trait at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Loop Audio? | Checked = loop audio after it finishes; unchecked = play once |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Audio Channel | The channel this Spark plays on. Use channel names to group and manage related audio. |
| Loop Audio? | When enabled, the clip repeats after finishing |

title: Countdown
content:
# Countdown

A Countdown Config is a countdown timer. It differs from the "Delay" Modifier in that it can be started, stopped, and queried mid-count — making it appropriate when you need to respond to the countdown reaching zero, or detect whether it is currently running.

To use: add a "Start" Effect to begin the countdown. Wire a "State Changed to" Cause (Condition: Expired) to fire when the countdown reaches zero.

---

## Causes

### State Changed to

Fires when the Countdown transitions to the specified state.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Condition | **Running** — countdown has started. **Stopped** — countdown was halted before expiring. **Expired** — countdown reached zero. |

### Value Changed

Fires on a recurring interval while the countdown is running. Use to update a display or trigger periodic checks during the countdown.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Interval (seconds) | How frequently the Cause fires during the countdown. A value of 1 fires once per second. |

---

## Effects

### Start

Begins the countdown from its current Length in Seconds value.

### Stop

Halts the countdown before it expires. Triggers "State Changed to" (Condition: Stopped) on any connected Causes.

### If State is

Conditional gate — passes the signal through only if the Countdown is currently in the specified state.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Condition | Running, Stopped, or Expired |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Length in Seconds | The duration of the countdown in seconds (default: 30) |

title: Datum
content:
# Datum

A Datum is a numeric variable — a named container for a single number. Use it to track scores, counts, health points, timers, or any numeric value that needs to change during a session and drive behavior or display.

Datum values can be displayed in the scene using a "Datum Viewer" Symbol Spark. To update the display, wire the Datum's "Updated" Cause to the "Datum Viewer" Symbol Spark's "Update" Effect.

A Datum's Current Value can survive a Chapter change if Is Persistent is enabled. This is the standard way to carry a value across Chapters — for example, routing a learner to a different debrief Chapter based on a choice made earlier, or accumulating a score across multiple scenes.

> **Two conditions must both be true for persistence to work:** the destination Chapter must contain a Datum Instance with **the exact same instance name**, and that instance must also have Is Persistent enabled. If either condition is not met, the value does not carry over and resets silently.

State Machine values do not persist across Chapter changes. When cross-Chapter memory is needed, use a Datum with Is Persistent — not a State Machine.

---

## Causes

### Updated

Fires each time the Current Value changes. Use to keep a display or downstream behavior synchronized with the latest value.

---

## Effects

### Math — Operations on a fixed number

| Effect | What it does | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| Set Value | Sets Current Value to a specified number | Value |
| Add Value | Adds to Current Value | Value |
| Subtract Value | Subtracts from Current Value | Value |
| Multiply Value | Multiplies Current Value | Value (factor) |
| Divide Value | Divides Current Value | Value (divisor) |
| Reset Value | Resets Current Value to Initial Value | — |

### Math — Operations using another Datum

| Effect | What it does | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| Set Datum | Sets Current Value to another Datum's Current Value | Datum Instance |
| Add Datum | Adds another Datum's value to this one | Datum Instance |
| Subtract Datum | Subtracts another Datum's value | Datum Instance |
| Multiply Datum | Multiplies by another Datum's value | Datum Instance |
| Divide Datum | Divides by another Datum's value | Datum Instance |

### Conditionals — Compare to a fixed number

Each conditional Effect has two outputs. Left output fires when the condition is true; right output fires when it is not.

| Effect | Left output fires when... | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| If Is Equal To Value | Current Value = specified value | Value |
| If Is Less Than Value | Current Value < specified value | Value |
| If Is Greater Than Value | Current Value > specified value | Value |

### Conditionals — Compare to another Datum

| Effect | Left output fires when... | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| If Is Equal To Datum | This value = other Datum's value | Datum Instance |
| If Is Less Than Datum | This value < other Datum's value | Datum Instance |
| If Is Greater Than Datum | This value > other Datum's value | Datum Instance |

### Modify

Sets a Datum trait at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Persistent | Checked = retain Current Value across Chapter reloads; unchecked = reset on reload |
| Initial Value | The starting value used when the Datum is first created or reset |
| Current Value | Sets the active value directly |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Persistent | When enabled, Current Value is retained when the Chapter reloads or changes |
| Initial Value | The starting value applied when the Datum is first created or reset |
| Current Value | The active value; changes in response to Effects and can drive Causes and displays |

title: Group
content:
# Group

A Group Config organizes multiple Spark Instances into a single logical unit, allowing collective visibility control with a single Effect node rather than wiring individual "Visible" Effects to each Spark.

---

## Effects

### Visible

Shows or hides all Spark Instances assigned to this Group.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = show all group members; unchecked = hide all group members |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Group Name | The name of this Group; also displays the Sparks currently assigned to it |

title: Inventory
content:
# Inventory

An Inventory Config stores a list of Spark Instance names — useful for tracking collected items, completed steps, or visited locations. The list can be displayed in the scene using an "Inventory Viewer" Symbol Spark.

**Behavior:**
- Items are stored by Spark Instance name
- No duplicate names — adding the same Spark again has no effect
- When Maximum Items is reached, the oldest item is removed to make room for the new one

To display the list: wire the "Changed" Cause to an "Inventory Viewer" Symbol Spark's "Update" Effect.

---

## Causes

### Changed

Fires whenever the inventory list is modified — items added or removed.

---

## Effects

### Add

Adds a Spark Instance name to the inventory list.

### Remove

Removes a specified Spark Instance name from the inventory list.

### Clear

Removes all items from the inventory list.

### Modify

Sets the Maximum Items trait at runtime.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Val. Int | The new Maximum Items value |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Maximum Items | The maximum number of items the Inventory can hold. When exceeded, the oldest item is removed. |

title: Randomizer
content:
# Randomizer

A Randomizer Config generates a random output from a defined range. It is more capable than the "Random" Modifier — it supports unique selection (each value used only once per cycle) and auto-reset, making it appropriate for randomizing training scenarios without repetition.

To use: call "Generate Value" to randomly fire one of the Randomizer's outputs. The number of available outputs is set by the Total Values trait.

---

## Causes

### No Valid Value

Fires when all values in the current cycle have been used. Only activates when Require Unique is enabled.

### On Last Valid Value

Fires when the last remaining value is about to be selected — one value remains before the cycle is exhausted. Only activates when Require Unique is enabled.

---

## Effects

### Generate Value

Randomly selects and fires one of the Randomizer's outputs. The number of available outputs is determined by the Total Values trait.

### Reset History

Clears the record of previously selected values, allowing the full range to be selected again.

### Set Valid Outputs

Updates the Valid Values trait — the number of values currently available for selection.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Valid Outputs | The new Valid Values count |

### Modify

Sets Randomizer traits at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Require Unique? | When enabled, each value is selected only once per cycle before repeating |
| Auto Reset History? | When enabled, selection history resets automatically after all values are used |
| Total Values | Total number of possible outputs the Randomizer can select from |
| Valid Values | Number of values currently available for selection in the active cycle |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Require Unique? | Prevents value repetition within a cycle — each output fires once before any can repeat |
| Auto Reset History? | Automatically resets the selection history when all values are exhausted |
| Total Values | Total number of possible outputs the Randomizer can select from |
| Valid Values | Current count of values available for selection in the active cycle |

title: Respawn
content:
# Respawn

A built-in Config Spark that cannot be added or removed from the scene. Respawn ensures that if the player falls below ground level, they are automatically repositioned to prevent infinite falling.

No configuration required. No Causes or Effects beyond the inherited base behaviors.

title: Skies
content:
# Skies

The Skies folder in the Spark Browser contains a library of preset skybox options for different lighting conditions: Day 1–4, Night 1–4, Rainy 1–4, Snowy 1–4, and Starry Sky.

**One Sky active at a time.** A Chapter can only have one active Sky. Dragging a second Sky into the scene replaces the current one.

Sky Sparks can be modified at runtime via behavior wiring to adjust ambient lighting conditions.

---

## Effects

### Modify

Adjusts Sky traits at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Ambient Brightness | Intensity of ambient (non-directional) light in the scene |
| Ambient from Sky | When enabled, derives ambient lighting color and intensity from the sky itself |
| Exposure | Overall exposure of the sky — higher values brighten the scene |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Ambient Brightness | Controls how bright the ambient light is in the environment |
| Ambient from Sky | When enabled, ambient light matches the sky's color and conditions |
| Exposure | Adjusts overall sky exposure — affects scene brightness |

title: State Machine (Named)
content:
# State Machine (Named)

A Named State Machine functions identically to the State Machine, but uses text names instead of numbers. States are defined by name — for example: Idle, Talking, Interacting — making behavior trees more readable in complex scenes.

**Important: "On State" fires automatically at chapter load.** The "On State" Cause for the first state in the list fires at Chapter start, before any user interaction.

**Important: Setting the same state again has no effect.** If the Named State Machine is set to a state it is already in, the "On State" Cause does not fire. Nothing happens.

---

## Causes

### On State

Fires when the Named State Machine transitions to the specified named state.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Name | The state name that triggers this Cause |

---

## Effects

### Go to Named State

Sets the current state to a specified named state.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Name | The named state to transition to |

### Next State

Advances to the next state in the Named State Machine's defined state list.

### Previous State

Moves to the previous state in the Named State Machine's defined state list.

### If State is Named

Conditional gate — passes the signal through only if the current state matches the specified name.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Name | The state name to compare against |

title: State Machine
content:
# State Machine

A State Machine Config tracks a numeric state value and gates or triggers behavior based on which state is currently active. States are whole numbers (0, 1, 2, 3...). The default state is 0.

Use State Machine for branching logic, multi-outcome scenarios, or any situation where behavior depends on what has already happened. The State Machine gives a behavior tree memory.

**Important: "On State" fires automatically at chapter load.** The "On State" Cause with State Id set to 0 fires at the start of every Chapter, before any user interaction. This is intentional and reliable — use it to initialize state-dependent behavior at chapter load.

**Important: Setting the same state again has no effect.** If a "Go to State" Effect sets the State Machine to a state it is already in, the "On State" Cause does not fire. Nothing happens.

---

## Causes

### On State

Fires when the State Machine transitions to the specified state.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Id | The whole number that triggers this Cause |

---

## Effects

### Go to State

Sets the current state to a specified value.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Id | The state to transition to |

### Next State

Increments the current state by 1. If current state is 2, this sets it to 3.

### Previous State

Decrements the current state by 1. If current state is 2, this sets it to 1.

### If State is

Conditional gate — passes the signal through only if the current state equals the specified value.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| State Id | The state value to compare against |

title: Sun
content:
# Sun

A built-in Config Spark that cannot be added or removed from the scene. The Sun acts as the primary directional light source. Its Brightness and Time of Day traits can be adjusted in the Traits Panel at authoring time or modified at runtime via behavior wiring.

---

## Effects

### Modify

Adjusts Sun traits at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Brightness | Light intensity as a percentage (0 = darkness, 100 = full brightness) |
| Time of Day | Hour in 24-hour format (0–24). Affects sun position and angle — 9 = 9am, 18 = 6pm |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Brightness (0–100) | Controls sunlight intensity as a percentage |
| Time of Day (0–24) | Sets the sun's position using a 24-hour clock |

title: Accessories
content:
# Accessories

*Advanced feature. Not covered in trial curriculum. Full documentation to be added post-launch.*

Accessory Sparks are Entity Sparks designed to attach to the player's body at runtime, typically used to build wrist-mounted UI in VR — a watch-style interface the player can glance at and interact with.

**Watch Band** — the visual strap component. Attaches to a specified body part (typically the left hand in VR) and aligns itself relative to the Watch Face. Set Is Attached to true in the Traits Panel or via behavior wiring to snap it to the player.

**Watch Face** — the interactive face of the watch. Also attaches to a body part via Is Attached. Supports a Billboard for displaying content and an "If Interacted" Effect for triggering actions when the player interacts with the watch — commonly used to open a menu or display status information.

### Shared Traits (Watch Band and Watch Face)

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Attached | When enabled, the Spark snaps to the player's body |
| Body Part | The body part to attach to (e.g., left hand) |
| Offset Position | Positional offset relative to the attachment point |
| Offset Rotation | Rotational offset relative to the attachment point |

title: Drawables
content:
# Drawables

*Advanced feature. Not covered in trial curriculum. Full documentation to be added post-launch.*

Drawable Sparks enable freehand drawing directly in the scene at runtime. The system consists of three cooperating Spark types:

**Drawable Surface** — a blank canvas Entity Spark that can be drawn on by a Marker Spark. Multiple Markers can draw on the same surface.

**Marker** — the drawing instrument. When it contacts a Drawable Surface, it renders a stroke. Configurable for color, pen size, stroke smoothness, and drawing distance. The Require Held trait controls whether the player must physically hold the Marker to draw, or whether it draws automatically on contact. A Marker can be attached invisibly to another Spark (with its color alpha set to 0 and Require Held unchecked) to allow non-Marker Sparks to draw on surfaces.

**Eraser** — removes strokes from a Drawable Surface one continuous stroke at a time.

### Key Marker Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Pen Color | RGBA color of the ink |
| Pen Size | Width of the stroke |
| Distance Between Points | Spacing between stroke points — lower values produce smoother curves (default: 0.01) |
| Require Held | When enabled, player must grip the Marker to draw; when disabled, draws on contact automatically |
| Max Drawing Distance | Maximum range at which the Marker renders on a surface (default: 0.03) |

title: Entity Spark Behaviors
content:
# Entity Spark Behaviors

All Entity Spark Instances share the same set of Causes and Effects. This page documents those behaviors. For Config Spark and Symbol Spark behaviors, see their individual reference pages. For Modifier behaviors (available in every Chapter), see the [Behavior Wiring Reference](../behavior-wiring-reference.md).

For an overview of how the Behaviors tab works, see [Behaviors tab](../ui-panels/behavior-panel.md).

---

## Causes

Causes are triggers. When a Cause's conditions are met, it fires its output and passes the signal downstream.

### Common Parameters

**One Shot**
Available on Approached, Collided, and Grabbed. When enabled, the Cause fires once — the first time its conditions are met — and then permanently deactivates for the remainder of the Chapter session. Use One Shot when an event should only happen once per session, such as playing an introductory animation.

**Prerequisite traits**
Some Causes require a corresponding trait to be enabled on the Instance before they can fire. If the prerequisite trait is not enabled, the Cause will never trigger. Builder displays a yellow warning triangle on a Cause node when it detects a missing prerequisite — but this warning is not consistently applied across all Causes. Always verify relevant traits in the Traits Panel directly. See [Warning Triangle Inconsistency](#warning-triangle-inconsistency) in the Notes section.

---

### On Started

Fires when this Entity Instance is initialized in the scene.

`[PENDING: confirm exact trigger condition — whether this fires on Chapter load, on Clone spawn, or both]`

**One output.**

---

### Approached

Fires when the player or a specified Spark Instance enters within a set distance of this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Distance | The proximity radius that triggers the Cause, in scene units (approximately meters) | 5 |
| Player | When enabled (X), fires when the player enters the zone | Enabled |
| Spark | When a Spark Instance is selected from the dropdown, also fires when that Instance enters the zone | None |
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

Both Player and Spark can be active simultaneously — the Cause fires when either condition is met.

**One output.**

---

### Collided

Fires when this Entity collides with another object in the scene.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| On Enter | Fire when the collision begins | Enabled |
| On Exit | Fire when the collision ends | Disabled |
| With Player | Fire when the collision involves the player | Enabled |
| With Spark | Fire when the collision involves a specific Spark Instance | Disabled |
| Left Hand | Fire specifically for left controller hand collisions | Disabled |
| Right Hand | Fire specifically for right controller hand collisions | Disabled |
| Threshold | Minimum time delay in seconds before a new collision can be registered after an initial detection | 0.1 |
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

**Threshold** prevents double-triggers from a single collision event. Increase it if you are seeing unintended repeated triggers.

**Prerequisite:** Is Collidable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. **Builder does not show a warning triangle when Is Collidable is disabled.** A Collided Cause with Is Collidable off will fail silently. Always verify Is Collidable when Collided is not behaving as expected.

**Held Sparks trigger collisions.** A Spark that the player is currently holding (grabbed) can still trigger Collided events when it makes contact with other objects. This means you can wire behaviors that respond to the player hitting something with a held object.

**One output.**

---

### Grabbed

Fires when this Entity is picked up or put down by the player.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

**Two outputs:**
- **Left output (On Grabbed):** fires when the player picks up the Entity
- **Right output (On Released):** fires when the player puts the Entity down

**Prerequisite:** Is Grabbable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. Builder shows a warning triangle when Is Grabbable is disabled.

**Grab direction constraint:** The player can only grab Sparks that are in front of them. A Spark directly behind the player cannot be picked up, even if it is within range and Is Grabbable is enabled.

---

### Interacted

Fires when the player activates this Entity. In VR, activation uses the laser pointer. In Builder play mode, press **E** while facing the object to simulate interaction.

No configurable parameters.

**Two outputs:**
- **Left output (Interact On):** fires when the player activates the Entity
- **Right output (Interact Off):** fires when the player deactivates the Entity

**Prerequisite:** Is Interactable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. Builder shows a warning triangle when Is Interactable is disabled.

> **Builder play mode distance limit:** You must be within approximately 1 meter of an object to interact with it in Builder play mode. This is more restrictive than VR. If pressing E does nothing, move closer and try again.

---

### Trait Is…

Fires when a specified trait on this Entity meets a defined condition.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to evaluate — select from this Instance's exposed traits |
| Condition | Equal To, Greater Than, or Less Than |
| Value | The value to compare against |

Greater Than and Less Than are only meaningful for numeric traits. For boolean traits, use Equal To.

**One output.**

---

## Effects

Effects are consequences. When wired to a Cause output, an Effect executes when the Cause fires.

---

### Animation

#### Animate Play

Starts a named animation on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Clip | The animation clip to play |
| Do Loop | When enabled, the animation loops continuously until stopped |

**Prerequisite:** The "Do Animation" trait must be enabled on this Spark Instance.

`[PENDING: confirm additional parameters (Material Name, Direction Obj., Speed) with developer]`

#### Animate Stop

Stops the currently playing animation on this Entity. No parameters.

---

### Attachment and Grab

#### Attach On

Attaches this Entity to another Spark Instance as a child object.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Type | What to attach to: **Spark**, **Player_Head**, **Player_Hand_L**, **Player_Hand_R** | Spark |
| Parent | When Type is Spark: the specific Spark Instance to attach to | None |
| Offset Position X/Y/Z | Position offset from the attachment point's origin | 0, 0, 0 |
| Offset Rotation X/Y/Z | Rotation offset from the attachment point's orientation | 0, 0, 0 |

#### Attach Off

Detaches this Entity from its current parent and returns it to world space. No parameters.

#### Force Grab

Places this Entity directly into the player's hand without requiring the player to pick it up manually.

`[PENDING: confirm whether Left/Right hand is configurable and where that parameter appears]`

#### Force Drop

Removes this Entity from the player's hand. No parameters.

---

### Appearance

#### Highlight

Adds or removes a pulsing blue highlight on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = highlight on; unchecked = highlight off | Unchecked |

**This is a state-setter, not a toggle.** See [Visible and Highlight Are State-Setters](#visible-and-highlight-are-state-setters) in the Notes section.

#### Visible

Shows or hides this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = visible; unchecked = hidden | Unchecked |

**This is a state-setter, not a toggle.**

> **Hidden objects cannot be interacted with.** A hidden Entity (Visible = off) will not respond to the "Interacted" Cause. Do not wire an "Interacted" Cause to a "Visible (off)" Effect expecting the player to interact with the hidden object to make it reappear — the interaction will never fire. Use a separate always-visible trigger object, or a different Cause such as "Approached". See [Toggle: Flip Between Two States](../wiring-behaviors/common-patterns.md#toggle-flip-between-two-states) for the correct pattern.

#### Sub Mesh

Shows or hides a named submesh within this Entity's 3D model.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| SubMesh | The name of the submesh to affect | (first available) |
| Visible | Checked = show submesh; unchecked = hide submesh | Unchecked |

Requires the Entity's source asset to have defined named submeshes.

---

### Transform

#### Move

Moves this Entity to a target position.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Set Altitude | When enabled, this node sets the Entity's vertical position | Enabled |
| Altitude | Target altitude value | 0 |
| Set Position | When enabled, this node sets the Entity's horizontal position | Enabled |
| Position X | Target horizontal position — X axis | 0 |
| Position Y | Target horizontal position — Y axis | 0 |
| Move Type | Absolute: move to a specific coordinate. Relative: move by an offset | Absolute |
| Time To Move | Duration of the movement in seconds | 1 |

#### Rotate

Rotates this Entity to a target orientation.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Rotation X | Target X-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotation Y | Target Y-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotation Z | Target Z-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotate Type | Absolute or Relative | Absolute |
| Time to Move | Duration of the rotation in seconds | 1 |

#### Scale

*Planned — not yet available.*

---

### Logic and Conditions

#### Modify

Sets the value of any exposed trait on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to modify |
| Value | The new value |

**Scale exception:** Modify does not support Scale for Entity Sparks.

#### If Trait Is…

A conditional gate. Passes the signal through only if the specified condition on this Instance is currently true.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to evaluate |
| Condition | Equal To, Greater Than, or Less Than |
| Value | The value to compare against |

**One output** — fires only when the condition evaluates to true.

#### Interactable

Enables or disables user interaction with this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = interactable; unchecked = not interactable | Unchecked |

---

### Lifecycle

#### Destroy

Removes this Entity Instance from the scene permanently for the remainder of the session. No parameters. Reloading the Chapter restores destroyed Instances.

#### Clone

Creates a new Instance of this Entity Spark in the scene at runtime. The clone appears at a specified spawn point. Use Clone to dynamically add objects during play — spawning projectiles, populating a scene based on player actions, or creating multiple copies of an object.

`[PENDING: confirm full parameter list — spawn point selection and any additional options]`

---

## Notes

### Warning Triangle Inconsistency

Builder shows a yellow warning triangle on Grabbed and Interacted when Is Grabbable or Is Interactable is disabled. **Collided does not show this warning when Is Collidable is disabled.** A Collided Cause with Is Collidable off will fail silently. Always verify Is Collidable directly in the Traits Panel.

---

### Visible and Highlight Are State-Setters

Both Visible and Highlight set a fixed state — they do not toggle. To show and then hide the same Entity, you need two separate Visible nodes wired to different Causes: one checked, one unchecked. If you need a single node that flips between states on each fire, use Toggle upstream with two separate Effects.

---

### Grabbed and Interacted Have Two Outputs

| Cause | Left output | Right output |
|---|---|---|
| Grabbed | On Grabbed (entity picked up) | On Released (entity put down) |
| Interacted | Interact On (player activates) | Interact Off (player deactivates) |

Wire each output independently to drive separate behavior paths from the same Cause node.

---

*Pending items require developer confirmation before publishing. Search for `[PENDING` to find all unresolved entries.*

title: Environment Sparks
content:
# Environment Sparks

Environment Sparks are invisible Entity Sparks — they are visible in Builder but not to the player at runtime. They serve structural and interactive roles in a scene: defining where the player starts, where they can travel, and what areas trigger behavior.

Environment Sparks participate in behavior trees using the standard Entity Spark Causes and Effects documented in [Entity Spark Behaviors](entity-spark-behaviors.md), unless noted otherwise below.

**Note:** Environment Sparks currently appear as a top-level folder in the Spark Browser alongside Entity Sparks. They are conceptually a subtype of Entity Spark.

---

## Light

A Light Spark adds a dynamic light source to the scene. It emits light from its position and can be adjusted for type, color temperature, and intensity.

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | **Point** — emits light in all directions from a single point. **Spot Light** — emits a cone of light, like a spotlight or flashlight. |
| Color Temperature | Adjusts the warmth or coolness of the light |
| Intensity | Controls the brightness of the light |

**Spot Light additional traits:**

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Direction | The direction the spotlight is pointing |
| Size Inner | The inner cone where light is at full intensity |
| Size Outer | The total spread of the spotlight beyond the inner cone |
| Range | How far the spotlight reaches |

---

## Portal

A Portal Spark is invisible to the player. It defines a destination point and teleports the player to that location when its "Teleport" Effect is triggered.

Common use: wire an "Approached" or "Collided" Cause on an invisible Trigger Spark to a Portal's "Teleport" Effect to create a seamless location transition.

### Effects

#### Teleport

Instantly moves the player to the Portal Spark's position.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Destination | The Spark Instance the player will be teleported to |

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Cooldown (s) | Wait time in seconds before the portal can be used again after teleportation (default: 0.5) |

> **Do not create mutual portal loops.** If Portal A teleports the player to Portal B, and Portal B is wired to teleport back to Portal A on the same collision trigger, the player will be teleported back and forth indefinitely. Always ensure portal destinations are one-directional, or add a gate (such as a State Machine or Interactable trigger) to control the return path.

---

## Reflection Probe

A Reflection Probe Spark captures the surrounding environment and applies dynamic reflections to nearby shiny surfaces — glass, mirrors, polished metal, and similar materials. Moving the Reflection Probe updates which environment it captures.

Works best with high-fidelity (HiFi) assets. Low-poly assets benefit less from reflection probes.

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Size | Adjusts the range of the reflection capture |

---

## Spawn Point

A Spawn Point Spark defines where the player appears when the Chapter loads or restarts. Without a Spawn Point, the player spawns at the scene origin (position 0, 0, 0).

Each Chapter supports one Spawn Point. Place it at the intended starting position and orientation for the player.

No Causes, Effects, or additional traits beyond the base Entity Spark behaviors.

---

## Trigger

A Trigger Spark is an invisible, non-rendering Entity Spark that functions as a sensor zone. It supports the full set of standard Entity Spark Causes — particularly "Approached" and "Collided" — making it ideal for activating behavior when the player enters a designated area without any visible object in the scene.

Use a Trigger when you need spatial detection but do not want a visible object in the scene.

No unique traits beyond the standard Entity Spark trait set.

title: Primitives
content:
# Primitives

Primitives are basic 3D shapes available in the Spark Browser. They behave as standard Entity Sparks — they have the full set of Entity Spark Causes, Effects, and Traits, and can participate in behavior trees like any other Entity Spark.

## Available Shapes

Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane, Quad, and others.

## Common Uses

**Prototyping and layout blocking** — Place Primitives to define spatial layout before final assets are imported. Swap with production assets when ready.

**Invisible collision boundaries** — Set Is Visible to off and Is Collidable to on to create invisible walls, floors, or barriers that prevent the player from walking through areas.

**Highlight indicators** — Use a semi-transparent Primitive to outline or highlight a region in the scene.

No unique Causes, Effects, or Traits beyond the standard Entity Spark set.

title: Button
content:
# Button

A Button Symbol is a pressable UI element. When the user presses it, it fires the "On Button Pressed" Cause, which can wire to any downstream Effect.

---

## Causes

### On Button Pressed

Fires when the button is pressed.

---

## Effects

### Visible

Shows or hides the button.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = visible; unchecked = hidden |

### Highlight

Applies or removes the highlighted visual state on the button.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = highlighted; unchecked = normal |

### Set Interactable

Enables or disables the button's ability to receive input.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Interactable | Checked = button responds to input; unchecked = button is visible but cannot be pressed |

### Modify

Sets Button traits at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Label Text | The text displayed on the button |
| Font Size | Size of the label text |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the label text |
| Background Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the button background |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
