| Label Text | The text displayed on the button (default: "Button") |
| Font Size | Size of the label text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the button |
| Is Interactable | Whether the button responds to input |
| Text Color | RGBA — label text color and opacity |
| Background Color | RGBA — default button background color |
| Highlight Color | RGBA — background color when the cursor hovers over the button |
| Pressed Color | RGBA — background color while the button is being pressed |
| Selected Color | RGBA — background color when the button is selected |
| Disabled Color | RGBA — background color when Is Interactable is off |

title: Countdown Viewer
content:
# Countdown Viewer

A Countdown Viewer Symbol displays the current value of a linked Countdown Config. The displayed value updates as the countdown runs.

To connect: wire the Countdown Config's "Value Changed" Cause to the Countdown Viewer's "Update" Effect.

---

## Effects

### Update

Refreshes the displayed countdown value. Wire this to the Countdown Config's "Value Changed" Cause to display the live countdown.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Font Name | The font used to render the value. "Default" uses the system font. |
| Font Size | Size of the displayed text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the Symbol's bounds |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the displayed value |
| Text Alignment | How text aligns within the Symbol's bounds (e.g., Top Left, Center) |

title: Crosshair
content:
# Crosshair

A Crosshair Symbol displays intersecting lines used as a visual aiming reference, typically in first-person mode. The highlight color changes automatically when the crosshair points at an interactable Spark.

No Causes or Effects. Configuration is through traits only.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Only Show First Person | When enabled, the crosshair is visible only in first-person mode and hidden in other views |
| Highlight Color | RGBA — color of the crosshair when pointing at an interactable Spark |

title: Datum Viewer
content:
# Datum Viewer

A Datum Viewer Symbol displays the current value of a linked Datum Config. The displayed value updates automatically when the "Update" Effect is triggered.

To connect a Datum Viewer to a Datum: wire the Datum's "Updated" Cause to the Datum Viewer's "Update" Effect. Then assign the Datum in the Datum Viewer's Datum trait.

---

## Effects

### Update

Refreshes the displayed value from the linked Datum. Wire this to the Datum's "Updated" Cause to keep the display synchronized.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Font Name | The font used to render the value. "Default" uses the system font. |
| Font Size | Size of the displayed text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the Symbol's bounds |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the displayed value |
| Text Alignment | How text aligns within the Symbol's bounds (e.g., Top Left, Center) |
| Datum | The Datum Config Instance whose value will be displayed |

title: Dropdown
content:
# Dropdown

A Dropdown Symbol displays a list of options that the user can select from, similar to a dropdown menu in a standard application interface.

Options can be defined at authoring time in the Options trait, or added and removed dynamically at runtime via Effects.

---

## Causes

### On Dropdown Changed

Fires when an option is selected, added, or removed from the dropdown.

---

## Effects

### Add Dropdown Option

Adds a new option to the dropdown list.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Option Name | The label for the new option — this is what appears in the dropdown menu |
| Allow Duplicates | When enabled, allows multiple options with the same name; when disabled, duplicate names are rejected |

### Remove Dropdown Option

Removes a specific option from the dropdown by name.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Option Name | The name of the option to remove |

### Clear Dropdown Options

Removes all options from the dropdown list.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Options | The list of options available in the dropdown |

title: Input Field
content:
# Input Field

An Input Field Symbol captures text typed by the user. It can be used to collect user-generated responses, search terms, or any freeform text input. Connect it to a "Text" Symbol via behavior wiring to display the entered text elsewhere in the UI.

---

## Causes

### On End Edit

Fires when the user finalizes their text entry (presses Enter or clicks away). Use to process or display the completed input.

### On Value Changed

Fires continuously as the user types. Use for real-time display or validation of input as it is entered.

---

## Effects

### Apply Value

Sends the current input field content to a linked "Text" Symbol.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Placeholder Text | Instructional text shown in the field before the user types anything |
| Text | The current text content of the input field |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the input text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the field |
| Is Interactable | When enabled, the field accepts input; when disabled, it is visible but read-only |
| Background Color | RGBA — default background color |
| Highlight Color | RGBA — background color on hover |
| Pressed Color | RGBA — background color when the field is active |
| Selected Color | RGBA — background color when the field is selected |
| Disabled Color | RGBA — background color when Is Interactable is off |

title: Inventory Viewer
content:
# Inventory Viewer

An Inventory Viewer Symbol displays the current contents of a linked Inventory Config. The list updates when the "Update" Effect is triggered.

To connect: wire the Inventory Config's "Changed" Cause to the Inventory Viewer's "Update" Effect.

---

## Effects

### Update

Refreshes the displayed inventory list. Wire this to the Inventory Config's "Changed" Cause to keep the display synchronized with the current inventory state.

title: 2D Primitives
content:
# 2D Primitives

2D Primitives are basic shapes for use inside UI containers (the Default HUD or a "Billboard" Entity Spark). They are building blocks for panels, backgrounds, dividers, highlights, and other visual UI elements.

No Causes or Effects. All configuration is through the common Symbol traits (Position, Size, Scale, Is Visible, etc.) plus color.

## Available Shapes

- Circle
- Circle (Half)
- Circle (Quarter)
- Diamond
- Oval
- Parallelogram
- Square
- Triangle (Equilateral)
- Triangle (Right)

title: Text
content:
# Text

A Text Symbol displays text in the UI. It can show static content (labels, instructions, signs) or be updated dynamically at runtime via behavior wiring.

---

## Effects

### Change Text

Replaces the current text content instantly.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| New Text | The text that replaces the existing content |

### Add Value To Text Number

Adds a specified number to the value currently displayed in the Text Symbol. Useful for running score displays. For example, if the text currently shows 5 and Value Added is 1, the display updates to 6.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Value Added | Amount to add to the current number |
| Decimal Places | Number of decimal places to display in the result |

### Change Number Over Time

Smoothly transitions the displayed number from its current value to a target value over a specified duration. For example, a score that counts up from 5 to 10 over 2 seconds.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Final Number | The target number to display after the transition |
| Time (s) | Duration of the transition in seconds |
| Decimal Places | Number of decimal places to display in the result |

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Text | The text content displayed by this Symbol |
| Font Name | The font used to render the text. "Default" uses the system font. |
| Font Size | Size of the text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the Symbol's bounds |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the text |
| Text Alignment | How text aligns within the Symbol's bounds (e.g., Top Left, Center) |

title: Toggle
content:
# Toggle

A Toggle Symbol is an on/off switch. It fires separate Causes for the on state, the off state, and any change — allowing different behavior to trigger depending on which way the toggle is switched.

---

## Causes

### On Toggle Changed

Fires whenever the toggle state changes in either direction. Use when you need to respond to any toggle interaction regardless of direction.

### On Toggle - On

Fires when the toggle is switched on.

### On Toggle - Off

Fires when the toggle is switched off.

---

## Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Text | Label text displayed alongside the toggle |
| Font Name | The font used to render the label. "Default" uses the system font. |
| Font Size | Size of the label text |
| Auto Font Size | When enabled, scales font size automatically to fit the Symbol's bounds |
| Text Color | RGBA — color and opacity of the label text |
| Text Alignment | How text aligns within the Symbol's bounds |

title: Behaviors tab
content:
# Behaviors tab

The Behaviors tab is the workspace for building behavior trees — the interactive logic of a scene. It is a chapter-wide canvas showing the complete behavior graph for the entire Chapter: every behavior node from every Spark Instance of every type (Entity, Config, Symbol, and Modifier) lives on this single shared canvas. Nodes from different Spark Instances wire together freely.

This is where you connect Causes to Effects. The Behaviors tab is available from both Map Editor and Map Explorer, but **behaviors only execute in play mode, which is only accessible from Map Explorer.** You can build and edit wiring from either view — but to test it, you must be in Map Explorer with play mode active.

## How the Canvas Works

The Behaviors tab canvas shows all behavior nodes for the current Chapter. Nodes are not filtered to the selected Spark Instance — the whole Chapter's behavior graph is always visible.

**Wiring connections** are made by dragging from an output dot at the bottom of a node to an input dot at the top of another node. Any output can connect to any input — there are no type restrictions. A chain can span multiple Spark Instances and Spark types freely.

## Adding Nodes

Three dropdowns appear at the top of the Behaviors tab: **Causes**, **Effects**, and **Modifiers**. These are add menus, not filters — selecting an item and pressing **+** adds a new node to the canvas.

**For Causes and Effects:** Use the Instance dropdown at the top of the panel to select the Spark Instance you want to add nodes from. The Causes and Effects dropdowns populate with that Instance's available behaviors. Select a type and press + to add it. Switch to a different Instance to add nodes from that Instance instead.

**For Modifiers:** The Modifiers dropdown is not tied to the selected Instance. Modifiers belong to the Modifier Spark (described below) — select a type and press + to add it regardless of what Instance is selected.

Once a node is on the canvas, the Instance dropdown has no further effect on it. Nodes already on the canvas are not filtered or hidden when you change the selected Instance.

### Selecting a Spark Instance

The Instance dropdown lists every Spark Instance present in the current Chapter. You do not need to use the dropdown directly — clicking a Spark Instance anywhere in the workspace updates the dropdown automatically:

- Click an Entity Spark Instance in the **Map Editor** or **Map Explorer**
- Click an Instance in the **Instances pane** — the Entities, Config, or Symbols tabs in the lower right of the workspace
- Click a UI element in the **UI Editor**

Any of these selections drives the same Instance dropdown. Choose whichever is most convenient for your current task. If you are positioning an object in the Map Editor and want to add a behavior to it, click it there — no need to hunt through the dropdown. If you need to select a Config Spark Instance that has no visible presence in the scene, use the Config tab in the Instances pane.

## The Modifier Spark

Modifiers are not behaviors of any Entity, Config, or Symbol Spark. They belong to a separate Modifier Spark that is permanently present in every Chapter — you do not add it yourself, and it cannot be removed. The Modifier Spark contains utility nodes: flow control (Delay, Toggle, Random), scene navigation (Change Chapter, Exit Book, Blackout), annotation (Comment), debugging (Debug), and others.

Because Modifiers belong to the Modifier Spark rather than a specific Spark Instance, the Modifiers dropdown always shows the same options regardless of what Instance is selected. The Causes and Effects dropdowns change based on the Instance selection. The three dropdowns look parallel, but the Modifiers dropdown behaves differently from the other two.

Modifier nodes appear on the shared Chapter canvas and wire into chains exactly like any other node.

## Canvas Navigation

Pan the canvas by holding the middle mouse button and dragging, or by right-clicking and dragging. Scroll to zoom. Use **Zoom to Fit Selected** to center the view on selected nodes, or **Zoom to Fit All** to see the full Chapter graph — useful for orienting yourself in large behavior trees.

## Chapter Started

"Chapter Started" is a special Modifier node that fires once when the Chapter loads, before any learner interaction. It is found in the Modifiers section, not in Causes, because it belongs to the Modifier Spark rather than any Instance. Use it as the starting point for initialization behaviors that must run at Chapter load — setting positions, establishing visibility states, or triggering audio that plays as the scene opens.

For a detailed explanation, see [Edit Mode vs. Play Mode](../confusion-shields/edit-play-mode.md), which covers when and why to use Chapter Started.

title: Gizmo
content:
# Gizmo

The Gizmo is the transform control that appears when you select a Spark Instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer. It lets you move, rotate, and scale the selected Instance directly in the viewport using color-coded handles — no mode switching required.

| Handle | Color | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Lines | Red, green, blue | Drag to move along a single axis |
| Squares | Red, green, blue | Drag to move within a plane (two axes simultaneously) |
| Arc | Green | Drag to rotate |
| Center box | White | Drag to scale uniformly (fixed ratio) |

The Gizmo always scales proportionally — there is no handle for non-uniform scaling. To set different scale values on individual axes, enter them directly in the Traits Panel.

For numeric precision on any transform, use the Traits Panel — enter exact values for Position, Altitude, Rotation, and Scale rather than dragging the Gizmo handles. The Gizmo is faster for approximate placement; the Traits Panel is more reliable for exact values.

title: Map Editor
content:
# Map Editor

The Map Editor is a construction view with a fixed camera for placing and positioning Spark Instances with precision. Use it when you are building and arranging your scene — placing objects, aligning them, and checking spatial relationships from consistent angles.

The Map Editor is for building. The Map Explorer is for testing. They show the same scene from different vantage points and with different tools available.

## Camera Orientations

The Map Editor offers seven camera orientations accessible from its toolbar:

| Orientation | What you see |
|---|---|
| Top Down | Looking straight down onto the scene floor |
| Bottom Up | Looking straight up from below the scene |
| North-South | Looking from north toward south |
| South-North | Looking from south toward north |
| East-West | Looking from east toward west |
| West-East | Looking from west toward east |
| Fly Cam | Free movement — position and angle the camera freely |

Switch between orientations to place Spark Instances accurately on all axes. A common workflow: use Top Down to set horizontal placement, then switch to North-South or East-West to adjust height.

## Snap

When Snap is enabled, Spark Instances move in grid increments rather than freely. Use Snap when precise alignment matters — for example, placing objects flush against walls or aligning objects to a shared baseline. Disable Snap when you need freeform placement.

## X-Ray Mode

X-Ray Mode moves the camera along a selected axis and cuts through the scene at that plane, making objects behind other objects visible. Use it when you need to see inside a complex scene — for example, viewing the interior of a machine or checking placement inside an enclosed space. X-Ray Mode affects the view only; it does not change the scene.

## Zoom Shortcuts

Two zoom shortcuts are available:

- **Zoom to Player** — moves the camera to the player's current position in the scene
- **Zoom to Selected** — moves the camera to focus on the currently selected Spark Instance

Use these to quickly navigate to a specific location without manually repositioning the camera.

## Navigation Controls

Camera controls differ between fixed camera modes and Fly Cam.

**Fixed camera modes (Top Down, Bottom Up, North-South, South-North, East-West, West-East):**

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| Right-click + drag | Pan within the camera plane |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in / out |

**Fly Cam:**

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| W / A / S / D | Move camera (relative to current camera orientation) |
| Left-click + drag | Look around (rotate camera) |
| E | Move camera up |
| Q | Move camera down |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in / out |

These are camera controls — you are moving and orienting the editor camera, not an avatar.

## Behaviors in Map Editor

Behaviors are never active in Map Editor. Wiring in the Behaviors tab exists and can be edited, but nothing executes. To test behaviors, switch to Map Explorer and enter play mode.

`[PENDING: implementation mid-April. Currently behaviors can fire outside of play mode — this is a known issue and is on the requirements list to fix before trial launch. The doc describes post-fix behavior.]`

title: Map Explorer
content:
# Map Explorer

The Map Explorer is a player-perspective view of the scene. The camera is attached to the player character. Use Map Explorer when you want to experience the scene the way a learner would — walking through it, testing interactions, and running behavior trees.

The Map Explorer is for testing and experiencing. The Map Editor is for constructing.

## Navigation Controls

Move through the scene using keyboard and mouse:

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| W / A / S / D or Arrow Keys | Move forward, left, back, right |
| Right-click + drag (two-finger click + drag on Mac trackpad) | Look around |
| E | Interact with an object *(play mode only)* |
| R | Grab an object *(play mode only)* |
| Space *(gravity off only)* | Move up |
| Option / Alt *(gravity off only)* | Move down |

Space and Option/Alt for vertical movement are only active when the physics toggle (gravity) is off. With gravity on, Space has no effect in Map Explorer.

The Interact (E) and Grab (R) keys trigger object behaviors. These only have effect in play mode — pressing them outside of play mode does nothing.

## Camera and View Modes

Map Explorer has a view mode dropdown in the toolbar that controls the camera perspective:

| Mode | Projection | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Fly Cam | Perspective | Free-movement camera; navigate the scene as a player would |
| Top Down | Orthographic | Looking straight down from above |
| Bottom Up | Orthographic | Looking straight up from below |
| North to South | Orthographic | Side view along the North–South axis |
| South to North | Orthographic | Opposite side view |
| East to West | Orthographic | Side view along the East–West axis |
| West to East | Orthographic | Opposite side view |

Fixed views (everything except Fly Cam) use orthographic projection — no perspective distortion, useful for precise alignment checking. Fly Cam uses perspective projection, which matches how the scene will appear to players.

You can rotate the camera freely in any view mode outside of play mode. Camera rotation in Map Explorer is independent from the camera in Map Editor — changing the view in one does not affect the other.

The default camera for player experience is **first person** — you see from the player's eye level. Third person is also available and can be changed in the Book settings. First person is the expected perspective for VR training content and is the appropriate default for most scenes.

## Testing Controls

Three buttons appear at the top of the Map Explorer viewport:

- **Physics toggle** — turns player physics (gravity, collision) on or off. Toggle physics off if you want to move through walls or fly through the scene without constraint during testing.
- **Reload Chapter** — reloads the current Chapter from saved state, including all Spark Instances and behavior trees. Use this to reset the scene during a test session without leaving Map Explorer.
- **Start Chapter** — launches the full Chapter experience as if a learner opened it. Use this to do a complete run-through from the beginning.

## Play Mode

Play mode is only available in Map Explorer. The **play button (triangle icon)** is in the bottom-right corner of the Map Explorer viewport. Clicking it enters play mode — all wired behaviors become active and respond to interaction. The button turns purple when play mode is active. To exit play mode, click the button again.

This means Map Editor is always in edit mode. There is no way to run behaviors from Map Editor. If behaviors are not responding during testing, verify you are in Map Explorer with play mode active.

For a complete explanation of how edit mode and play mode differ and what each is for, see [Edit Mode vs. Play Mode](../confusion-shields/edit-play-mode.md).

**Note:** A "Reset on Stop" checkbox currently appears in Map Explorer but has no effect. Stopping play mode always reloads the Chapter from its last saved state on disk. The checkbox will be removed in a future update — ignore it.

> **Wait for all loading indicators to clear before interacting.** When a Chapter is loading, one or more loading popups appear on screen. If you attempt to interact with the scene before all of them have finished, the application can get stuck. Wait until the loading UI is fully gone before navigating or triggering behaviors.

title: Spark Browser
content:
# Spark Browser

The Spark Browser is your library of everything available to place in a scene. All Sparks — Entity, Config, Symbol, and Environment — are organized here in folders. You drag Sparks from the browser into the Map Editor or Map Explorer to create Spark Instances.

Everything you add to a scene begins here.

### Browsing and Finding Sparks

Sparks are organized in top-level folders by type:

- **Entity Sparks** — 3D objects you place in the scene
- **Config Sparks** — logic and configuration elements with no physical presence
- **Symbol Sparks** — 2D interface elements used in UI Panels

Within each folder, Sparks are organized into subfolders. Browse by expanding folders. To place a Spark, drag it from the browser into the Map Editor or into the Map Explorer viewport.

**Environment Sparks** currently appear as their own top-level folder alongside Entity, Config, and Symbol Sparks. Environment Sparks are technically a subtype of Entity Spark — this placement is recognized as potentially misleading. A UI cleanup to move Environment Sparks inside the Entity Sparks folder is planned before trial launch.

**My Sparks** is a personal folder where Sparks you have created or imported are stored. It is separate from the built-in Spark library and is yours to organize as needed.

### Search

The Spark Browser has a search field. Searching returns matching Sparks by name. **Search results show the Spark name only — they do not show the folder path.** If you need to know where a Spark lives in the folder hierarchy, browse to it manually. The ability to show the folder path in search results is a planned feature.

### Organizing Your Sparks

Within My Sparks, you can create folders to organize your Sparks:

- **"Create Local Directory"** — creates a folder inside My Sparks. This is a standard folder for organization only — it has no special file system behavior. A rename to "New Folder" is under consideration.
- **"Export Spark"** — saves a Spark to any location on your local drive. Low expected usage — the primary reason to use this is sharing a Spark file with another author outside of platform sync.

### Asset Config

The "Asset Config" button in the Spark Browser is a placeholder for an upcoming feature: an org-specific asset library that will let your organization's custom assets appear directly in the browser. It does not currently route to an active destination. You can safely ignore it.

title: Traits Panel
content:
# Traits Panel

The Traits Panel shows the configurable properties of the currently selected Spark Instance. Every Spark Instance has traits — values that define how it looks, behaves, and participates in behavior trees.

Select a Spark Instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer to see its traits here.

> **Multi-select clears the panel.** If more than one Spark Instance is selected, the Traits Panel shows nothing. To view or edit traits, select one Instance at a time.

## What Traits Are

Traits are instance-specific property overrides. A Spark defines a set of properties as a template; a Spark Instance inherits those properties but can have individual values that differ from the template default. Changes made in the Traits Panel apply only to the selected Instance — they do not affect the Spark definition or any other Instance of the same Spark.

Common traits for Entity Spark Instances include:

- **Is Visible** — whether the object is visible when the Chapter loads
- **Is Interactable** — whether the player can activate the object with the laser pointer
- **Is Grabbable** — whether the player can pick up the object
- **Is Collidable** — whether physics collisions are registered for this object
- **Position, Altitude, Rotation, Scale** — the object's transform in the scene

Other Sparks expose different traits. A Config Spark like a State Machine exposes its defined states and starting state. An Audio Config Spark exposes its audio file and channel settings.

## Editing Traits Directly

You can type values directly into any trait field in the Traits Panel. Click the field and enter the value — the change applies immediately to the selected Instance.

This is the primary way to set precise values. The Gizmo lets you move, rotate, and scale objects by dragging in the scene, which is useful for rough placement and spatial judgment. When you need an exact number — a specific position coordinate, a rotation of exactly 90 degrees, a scale of 0.5 — type it directly into the Traits Panel.

**Position, Rotation, and Scale** are the most common traits edited this way. Each is exposed as individual X, Y, and Z fields. Common use cases:

- Snapping an object to a known coordinate after rough placement with the Gizmo
- Recording the exact coordinates of two positions to use later in a Move Effect
- Setting uniform scale across all axes without relying on drag handles
- Resetting rotation to zero after adjusting orientation in the scene

The two approaches are complementary. Use the Gizmo to get an object roughly where you want it, then use the Traits Panel to dial in the exact values.

## Traits and the Behaviors tab

Several Causes in the Behaviors tab require a corresponding trait to be enabled before they can fire. The Grabbed Cause requires Is Grabbable. The Interacted Cause requires Is Interactable. The Collided Cause requires Is Collidable.

**If a Cause is not firing, check the Traits Panel first.** A Cause whose prerequisite trait is disabled will fail silently in most cases — the behavior tree runs but nothing happens. Verifying traits directly is always faster than debugging the behavior tree first.

## Traits and Edit Mode

In edit mode, trait values in the Traits Panel represent the saved initial state of the scene. What you see in the Traits Panel is what a learner sees when the Chapter loads. If you modify a trait during testing in play mode, that change is not saved — when you exit play mode, the trait returns to its edit mode value.

title: UI Editor
content:
# UI Editor

The UI Editor is the authoring workspace for building 2D interface content displayed on a Billboard Spark Instance. Use it to design the flat UI layer — buttons, text, images, and other Symbol Spark elements — that a Billboard shows in the 3D scene.

The UI Editor is only active when a Billboard Spark Instance is selected in the dropdown at the upper right of the panel.

## Step 1 — Add a Billboard to the Scene

Open the Spark Browser and navigate to **Symbols / UI Containers**. You will find two Billboard types:

- **Billboard** — placed at a fixed position in world space. The learner must be facing it to see it.
- **Follow Head Billboard** — attached to the learner's view and always visible regardless of where they are in the environment. Use this for persistent HUD elements or instructions that must always be readable.

Drag the Billboard type you want into the scene from the Spark Browser, or drop it directly into the Map Explorer.

**Rename the Instance immediately.** Scenes with multiple Billboards become difficult to manage if they all have default names. Set a descriptive Instance Name in the Traits Panel as soon as the Billboard is placed.

## Step 2 — Configure Billboard Traits

With the Billboard Instance selected, the Traits Panel shows several configuration options:

**Canvas Resolution (X, Y)** — sets the pixel dimensions of the Billboard's surface. This controls the resolution of the 2D canvas, not the physical size of the object in the scene. Default is 1920 × 1080. Adjust the physical size using the Scale trait or the Gizmo.

**Background Color** — sets the background color of the Billboard canvas.

**Rotate towards camera** — when enabled, the Billboard automatically rotates so its front face always points at the player's camera. Useful for Billboards placed in the scene that should always be readable regardless of where the player is standing.

**Lock X Auto-Rotate / Lock Y Auto-Rotate** — constrains the auto-rotation axis when Rotate towards camera is enabled. Locking the X axis is the most common setting: the Billboard can spin horizontally to face the player but will not tilt up or down. Locking Y prevents horizontal rotation while allowing tilt.

**Rotation** — for a standard Billboard (Rotate towards camera disabled), you will need to set rotation manually. Billboards only display content on one face, and it can be difficult to tell which side is the front when the canvas is empty. Consider adding a Symbol Spark first so the front face becomes visible, then adjust rotation.

## Step 3 — Open the UI Editor

Click the **UI Editor** tab in the top navigation bar. In the upper right of the UI Editor panel, a dropdown lists every Billboard Instance in the current Chapter. Select the Billboard you want to edit. The canvas for that Billboard appears in the editor.

**Hidden Billboard gotcha:** If a Billboard's visibility is set to hidden in the scene, it will also be invisible in the UI Editor — you will see a blank canvas with no content visible to interact with. To edit a hidden Billboard, use the **Is Visible** toggle in the upper left of the UI Editor (this is a shortcut to set the Billboard's visibility trait to true). Make your edits, then remember to re-hide the Billboard when you are done. This is a known issue with no current fix scheduled.

## Step 4 — Add and Arrange Symbol Sparks

With a Billboard selected in the UI Editor dropdown, the Spark Browser displays the Symbol Sparks library. Drag Symbol Sparks from the browser directly onto the Billboard canvas. Once placed, you can:

- **Move** — drag the element to reposition it on the canvas
- **Resize** — drag the handles to scale the element
- **Select** — click to select and edit properties in the Traits Panel

Symbol Sparks placed in the UI Editor become Instances tracked in the Symbols tab of the Instances pane, the same as any other Spark Instance.

**Image backgrounds:** To use an image as a background or decorative element on a Billboard, import the image as an **ImageViewer Spark**. See *(ImageViewer Spark reference — forthcoming)* for import details.

## Step 5 — Wire Behaviors

Switch to the **Behaviors tab** to wire Causes and Effects for the Symbol Spark Instances on the Billboard. The UI Editor handles layout and composition; the Behaviors tab handles interactive logic. Neither alone is sufficient to build an interactive UI element.

For example: to make a button navigate to the next Chapter, select the Button Instance in the Behaviors tab, add an **On Button Pressed** Cause, and wire it to a **Change Chapter** Effect.

Causes, Effects, and parameters specific to each Symbol Spark type are documented in the individual Symbol Spark reference pages.

title: Causes and Effects
content:
# Causes and Effects

Every behavior in Pixo Builder starts with a Cause and ends with one or more Effects. Understanding what each does and how they connect is the foundation of all behavior wiring.

---

## Causes

A Cause is an event listener. It sits at the top of a behavior tree and fires when something specific happens — the player interacts with an object, an object enters a proximity radius, a trait changes value. A behavior tree always begins with a Cause; you cannot start a tree with an Effect.

When a Cause fires, it sends a signal down any wires connected to its output dot. Everything connected downstream executes.

## Effects

An Effect is an action. It receives a signal through its input dot and does something — changes a trait value, shows or hides an object, moves an object to a new position. Effects can also be chained: one Effect's output dot connects to the next Effect's input dot, creating a sequence.

## Where wiring happens

All wiring and node management happens exclusively in the **Behavior Panel** (the Behaviors tab in the left panel). You cannot add, remove, or wire nodes from the Map Editor or Map Explorer.

The Map Editor and Map Explorer are used to **select a Spark Instance**. Once an instance is selected, the Behavior Panel updates to show that instance's behaviors — where you then add Causes, add Effects, and wire them together.

The workflow is always:
1. Select a Spark Instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer.
2. Go to the Behavior Panel to add nodes and wire behaviors.

## How wiring works

Every node — Cause and Effect alike — has an **output dot** at its bottom and an **input dot** at its top.

A node's output is **invoked when the node completes**:
- A Cause's output is invoked when its trigger event occurs.
- An Effect's output is invoked when the effect finishes executing — when the highlight turns on, the object finishes moving, the number increments.

This is what makes behavior trees possible. Wire a Cause to an Effect, then wire that Effect's output to the next Effect, and so on. Each node completes and passes the signal forward. A "Delay" Effect, for example, completes after N seconds — which is what pauses the chain.

To connect two nodes:
1. Click and drag from an output dot.
2. Drag toward the input dot of the node you want to connect to.
3. Release when the wire snaps into place. The wire auto-connects when dragged close enough.

To delete a wire: click it to select it and press Delete, or drag one end off its dot.

To reconnect a wire: drag either end to a new dot.

Multiple Causes can connect to the same Effect input dot — both independently drive the same downstream tree.

Wiring is not limited to a single Spark Instance. Any output dot can connect to any input dot, regardless of which Instance each node belongs to. A Cause on one Instance can drive an Effect on any other Instance in the scene.

---

## Base Spark behaviors

These behaviors are available on every Spark, regardless of type.

**"Trait Is…" (Cause)** — fires when a specified trait on the instance meets a condition (equals, greater than, less than, etc.). Use this to trigger behavior in response to a trait change.

**"If Trait Is…" (Effect)** — a conditional gate. When it receives a signal, it checks whether a specified trait meets a condition. If the condition is true, the signal passes through to the next node; if false, nothing happens downstream.

**"Modify" (Effect)** — sets any exposed trait to a specified value at runtime. Use this to change an object's position, color, size, or any other trait without scripting.

---

Spark-specific Causes and Effects are documented in the [reference section](../../reference/).

title: Common Patterns
content:
# Common Patterns

These are recurring wiring patterns that appear across many different Builder projects. Each one solves a specific problem that comes up regularly. This page will grow as more usage patterns emerge from real projects.

---

## Initialization: Chapter Started

**Problem:** You need the scene to be in a specific state when it loads — objects hidden, interactions disabled, positions set — but Builder does not store a separate initial state.

**Pattern:** Use a "Chapter Started" Cause (from the Modifiers row) at the start of a behavior tree. Wire it to "Modify", "Visible", "Interactable", or any other Effect that sets an Instance to its correct starting state. This tree runs once, automatically, when the Chapter loads.

```
Chapter Started → Visible (unchecked) → Interactable (unchecked)
```

Use this for every piece of state that matters at Chapter start. It is the standard solution to the No Initial State problem and a habit worth building early.

---

## Timed Sequence: Delay

**Problem:** You want something to happen, then something else to happen after a pause.

**Pattern:** Insert a "Delay" Effect between two nodes. The Delay's output is invoked after the specified number of seconds, passing the signal to whatever is wired downstream.

```
Interacted → Highlight (on) → Delay (2 seconds) → Highlight (off)
```

Delay only pauses the chain it belongs to — other behavior trees in the scene continue running normally.

---

## Toggle: Flip Between Two States

**Problem:** A single trigger (one button, one interaction) needs to alternate between two states — show/hide, on/off — each time it fires.

**Pattern:** Wire the Cause to a "Toggle" Effect (from Modifiers). "Toggle" has two outputs that alternate on each invocation. Wire one output to the "on" state Effect and the other to the "off" state Effect.

```
Interacted (Interact On) → Toggle → [left output] Visible (checked)
                                  → [right output] Visible (unchecked)
```

Use this for "Highlight" and similar state-setters that need to flip on a single trigger.

> **Do not use Toggle + Visible with an "Interacted" Cause on the same object.** When the object is hidden (Visible = off), it cannot be interacted with — so the second click never fires. The toggle becomes a one-way trip: the object disappears and cannot be brought back via interaction. To toggle visibility, use a separate always-visible trigger object, or a different Cause such as "Approached."

---

## Multiple Triggers, One Result

**Problem:** Several different events should all produce the same outcome.

**Pattern:** Wire multiple Cause outputs into the same Effect input dot. Each Cause independently invokes the downstream tree when it fires.

```
Approached →
              Highlight (on)
Interacted →
```

Any number of Causes can feed the same Effect. This avoids duplicating Effect nodes and keeps the canvas clean.

---

## Chained Effects: Sequence

**Problem:** You need a series of things to happen in order after a single trigger.

**Pattern:** Wire the Cause to Effect 1. Wire Effect 1's output to Effect 2. Wire Effect 2's output to Effect 3. Each Effect's output is invoked when it completes, passing the signal to the next node in the chain.

```
Interacted → Animate Play → Delay (1 second) → Visible (unchecked) → Change Chapter
```

This pattern is the basis of most training interactions: trigger, feedback, pause, transition.

---

## Conditional Branch: If Trait Is

**Problem:** The same trigger should produce different results depending on the current state of the scene.

**Pattern:** Insert an "If Trait Is…" Effect into the chain. It passes the signal through only if its condition evaluates to true at the moment it is invoked. Wire separate paths for different conditions.

```
Interacted → If Trait Is… (counter = 3) → Change Chapter
```

Use this to gate progression — only advance when a specific condition has been met.

---

## Scene Exit: Change Chapter

**Problem:** You need to end the current Chapter and move the player to the next one.

**Pattern:** Wire any Cause to a "Change Chapter" Effect (from Modifiers). Select the target Chapter in the node's parameter. This is the standard way to build multi-Chapter experiences and completion flows.

```
Interacted → Change Chapter (select target)
```

To end the experience entirely, use "Exit Book" instead.

---

## Confirming a Chain Fired: Debug

**Problem:** A behavior is not producing the expected result and you cannot tell where the chain is breaking.

**Pattern:** Insert a "Debug" Effect at the point in the chain you want to verify. It sends a custom message to the Console when invoked. Move the node up or down the chain to isolate where the signal stops.

```
Interacted → Debug ("Interacted fired") → Highlight (on) → Debug ("Highlight reached")
```

See [Debugging Behaviors](debugging-behaviors.md) for the full troubleshooting workflow.

title: Debugging Behaviors
content:
# Debugging Behaviors

When a behavior does not fire as expected, the problem usually falls into one of a few categories: a missing prerequisite trait, a behavior tested in the wrong mode, or a wiring error that is not immediately visible. This page covers the tools available and the most common things to check.

---

## The Console

The Console displays errors and warnings generated at runtime, each with a timestamp. Open it from the toolbar. Use the filter controls to show only errors, only warnings, or all messages. "Clear" removes existing messages. "Collapse" groups repeated messages to reduce noise.

Check the Console immediately when a behavior does not fire — errors from missing prerequisites or misconfigured nodes appear here.

---

## The Debug node

The "Debug" Modifier Effect sends a custom text message to the Console when it receives a signal, along with the name of the Spark Instance that triggered it. Place a "Debug" node at any point in a behavior chain to confirm whether the signal is reaching that point — the Console output will show both your message and which Instance fired it, making it easier to trace chains that span multiple Instances.

**How to use it:**

1. Add a "Debug" node from the Modifiers row in the "Behaviors" panel.
2. Connect it at the point in the chain you want to verify — between two nodes, or at the end of a tree.
3. Enter a descriptive message on the node (e.g., "Interacted fired", "Highlight reached").
4. Enter play mode and trigger the behavior.
5. Check the Console. If you see the message, the signal reached that node. If you do not, the chain is breaking upstream.

"Debug" nodes have no effect on player experience. Leave them in place during development and remove them before publishing, or keep them — they are silent to players.

---

## Warning triangles

A yellow warning triangle on a Cause node indicates a missing prerequisite trait. The node will not fire until the trait is enabled.

- "Grabbed" requires "Is Grabbable" on the instance.
- "Interacted" requires "Is Interactable" on the instance.

**Exception: "Collided" does not show a warning triangle** when "Is Collidable" is off. If a "Collided" Cause never fires, check "Is Collidable" on the instance manually — it fails silently without any visual indicator in Builder.

---

## Prerequisite traits checklist

If a Cause is not firing, verify the following traits are enabled on the relevant instance in the "Traits" tab:

| Cause | Required trait |
|---|---|
| "Interacted" | Is Interactable |
| "Grabbed" | Is Grabbable |
| "Collided" | Is Collidable (no warning shown if missing) |

---

## Edit mode vs. play mode

Behaviors do not run in edit mode. This is the most common reason a behavior appears to do nothing during development.

To test any behavior:

1. Click the triangle (play) button in the bottom-right of the Map Explorer. The button turns purple when play mode is active.
2. Trigger the Cause in the scene.
3. Click the stop button to return to edit mode.

If a behavior works in play mode but appears broken in edit mode, that is expected. Edit mode is for building; play mode is for testing.

---

## Common troubleshooting steps

1. **Nothing happens when I trigger the Cause.** Check that you are in play mode. Check that the prerequisite trait is enabled. Check the Console for errors. If using "Interacted", confirm you are within approximately 1 meter of the object — Builder play mode has a shorter interaction range than VR. Move closer and try again.
2. **"Collided" never fires.** Enable "Is Collidable" on the instance. Builder will not warn you that it is missing.
3. **The behavior fires once but not again.** Check whether "One Shot" is enabled on the Cause. One Shot permanently deactivates the Cause after the first fire for that Chapter session.
4. **A sequence stops partway through.** Add "Debug" nodes after each step to find where the signal stops. Check "If Trait Is…" nodes — a false condition silently blocks the signal.
5. **Effects run but produce no visible result.** Confirm the Effect parameters are set correctly (e.g., the "Enabled" checkbox on "Highlight" or "Visible"). Confirm you are targeting the right instance.
6. **"Interacted" stopped firing after the object was hidden.** A hidden object (Visible = off) cannot be interacted with. If you hid an object and expected the player to interact with it to make it reappear, that interaction will never fire. Use a separate always-visible trigger object, or a different Cause such as "Approached". See the [Toggle pattern](common-patterns.md#toggle-flip-between-two-states) for the correct approach.

title: Modifiers
content:
# Modifiers

The Modifier Spark is a special built-in Config Spark that is permanently present in every Chapter. You do not place it from the Spark Browser — it is always available. Access its behaviors through the "Modifiers" row in the "Behaviors" panel, separate from any Spark Instance you have selected.

Modifiers handle scene-level logic: initialization, navigation between Chapters, timing, flow control, and debugging. These behaviors have no physical presence in the scene; they act on the Chapter or experience as a whole.

---

## Scene initialization

**"Chapter Started" (Cause)** — fires once, automatically, when the Chapter loads. Wire this Cause to any Effects that need to run at the start of every session: setting initial visibility, enabling or disabling interactability, positioning objects, or any other state that should be established before the player acts.

"Chapter Started" is the standard solution to Builder's No Initial State problem. Builder does not store a separate initial state apart from the scene itself. If you move or modify an instance during testing and save, that becomes the new starting position. To guarantee a known starting state regardless of how testing was done, use "Chapter Started" to explicitly set every critical trait value when the Chapter loads.

---

## Navigation and scene flow

**"Change Chapter" (Effect)** — navigates the player to another Chapter in the same Book. Parameter: Chapter (select from list).

**"Exit Book" (Effect)** — ends the experience and returns the player to the Pixo Platform. No parameters.

**"Blackout" (Effect)** — applies a full-screen fade. Parameter: Type — "FadeOut" (fade to black), "FadeIn" (fade from black), or "FadeOutThenIn" (fade out, then back in). Use "Blackout" to mask scene transitions or object repositioning.

---

## Flow control

**"Delay" (Effect)** — pauses the behavior chain for a specified number of seconds before passing the signal to the next node. Default: 5 seconds. The delay affects only the chain it is part of; other behavior trees in the scene continue running normally.

**"Toggle" (Effect)** — routes the signal to one of two outputs, alternating each time it fires. First fire goes to the left output, second to the right, third to the left again, and so on. Use "Toggle" upstream of state-setter Effects (like "Visible" or "Highlight") when you need a single trigger to flip between two states.

**"Random" (Effect)** — routes the signal to one of N outputs chosen at random each time it fires. Parameter: Output Count (default 2). Use this to introduce unpredictability into a behavior sequence.

---

## Utility

**"Debug" (Effect)** — sends a custom text message to the Console when triggered. Use "Debug" nodes during development to confirm that a behavior chain is firing as expected. Remove or leave them in place — they have no effect on the player experience.

**"Stop Audio Channel" (Effect)** — stops all audio playing on a named channel.

**"Comment"** — an annotation node with no effect on behavior execution. Use it to leave notes on the canvas about what a behavior tree does. Comments appear only in the editor; players never see them.

---

## Advanced: Action and Ember

**"Action" (Cause)** — fires when the player presses a specific controller input (Attack, Crouch, Grab, Interact, Jump, or Laser). This is a global listener: it fires anywhere in the scene, not tied to a specific object. Useful for building controller-driven interactions that are not tied to a physical object. This is an advanced behavior — plan carefully when global input listeners interact with object-level behaviors.

**Ember** — the Ember tab in the left panel exposes scripting capabilities for advanced logic. It is separate from the Modifier Spark and is covered in the Ember section of this documentation.

---

For full parameter details on all Modifier behaviors, see the [Modifiers reference](../../reference/modifiers/).

title: Organizing Your Canvas
content:
# Organizing Your Canvas

A behavior canvas with a handful of nodes is easy to read. As a Chapter grows — more Sparks, more conditions, more sequences — trees can spread across the canvas and become difficult to navigate. The canvas tools in the "Behaviors" panel help you keep things manageable.

---

## Group and Ungroup

Select multiple nodes and use the **Group** control to group them together. Grouped nodes move as a unit, making it easier to reposition a section of a behavior tree without manually selecting every node. Use **Ungroup** to dissolve the grouping.

Groups are visual and organizational only. They do not affect how behavior logic executes.

---

## Comment

A Comment is an annotation node you place directly on the canvas. It displays text and has no effect on behavior execution. Use Comments to label sections of a tree, note why a particular pattern was used, or flag something for review.

Comments are also available as a Modifier behavior from the Modifiers row — adding one from there places a Comment node on the canvas in the same way.

---

## Sub Graph

A Sub Graph collapses a selection of nodes into a single labeled block. The block shows the name you give it and hides the internal nodes from view. Click the block to expand and inspect or edit its contents.

Sub Graphs are organizational only. The behavior logic inside executes exactly as it would if the nodes were expanded. Collapsing nodes into Sub Graphs does not change timing, order of execution, or any other behavior.

Use Sub Graphs to:
- Hide the internals of a completed, working sequence you do not need to edit regularly.
- Group a logical unit (an initialization tree, a feedback sequence) under a readable name.
- Reduce the number of visible nodes on the canvas and recover editor performance.

> Collapsing nodes into Sub Graphs is the most effective way to improve Builder performance on dense canvases. Unorganized canvases with many visible nodes can slow the editor — Sub Graphs hide that complexity without changing how the logic executes.

title: State Machines
content:
# State Machines

A State Machine gives a behavior tree memory. Without one, every wired Cause fires the same Effect every time — there is no sense of "what has already happened" or "which step the learner is on." A State Machine tracks a current state, and lets you wire different behavior to each state. When the State Machine transitions, the scene responds accordingly.

State Machines are Config Sparks — they have no physical presence in the scene. You place one in the scene like any other Spark and wire to it from the Behaviors tab.

---

## When to use a State Machine

**Use direct wiring** when behavior is unconditional — when something should always happen whenever a trigger fires, regardless of anything else going on in the scene.

**Use a State Machine** when behavior should differ based on what has already happened. Common situations:

- A multi-step procedure where each step must be completed before the next one unlocks.
- A branching scenario where a learner's choice determines what happens at the end of the Chapter.
- An object or character that behaves differently at each stage of an interaction.
- Multiple Sparks that all need to respond to the same "phase" of a scene — you change one State Machine rather than re-wiring each Spark individually.

If you find yourself stacking multiple "If Trait Is…" gates to approximate a sequence, that is usually a signal to use a State Machine instead. The result will be easier to read and maintain.

---

## How State Machines work

### States

A State Machine tracks one value at a time: the current state. In a **State Machine**, states are whole numbers — 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. The default state is 0. In a **State Machine (Named)**, states are text names you define — for example: Idle, Talking, Complete.

The State Machine does not cycle or advance automatically. Nothing happens until something in your behavior tree explicitly triggers a transition.

### Transitioning between states

To change the current state, wire a **Go to State** (or **Go to Named State**) Effect to whatever Cause should trigger the transition. When that Effect fires, the State Machine updates its current value and fires the corresponding **On State** Cause.

You can also use **Next State** and **Previous State** Effects to increment or decrement through states in order, without specifying an explicit target — useful for linear sequences.

### The On State Cause

The **On State** Cause is what lets the rest of the scene respond to a state change. Wire it to any Effect you want to trigger when the State Machine enters that state.

A single State Machine can have multiple **On State** nodes in the Behaviors tab — one for each state you care about. Each fires only when the State Machine transitions to that specific state.

---

## State Machine vs. State Machine (Named)

Both Config Sparks work identically. The difference is readability.

| | State Machine | State Machine (Named) |
|---|---|---|
| State values | Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3 | Text names: Idle, Active, Done |
| Best for | Short sequences, counters, procedural logic | Branching scenarios, character states, anything that benefits from descriptive labels |
| Canvas readability | Compact, but requires mental mapping | Self-documenting — the state name tells you what it means |

For simple two- or three-state sequences, numeric states are fine. As scenes grow more complex, Named States make the Behaviors tab significantly easier to read and maintain.

---

## Worked example: multi-step procedure

A training scene requires the learner to close a valve before activating a switch. The switch should not respond until the valve has been closed.

**Setup:** Place one State Machine Config Spark. It starts at state 0 (valve open, switch locked).

**Tree 1 — Valve:**
```
Interacted (valve) → Go to State (1)
```

**Tree 2 — State Machine response:**
```
On State (1) → Interactable (switch, enabled)
```

**Tree 3 — Switch (only works after state 1):**
```
Interacted (switch) → [downstream effects]
```

Without the State Machine, you would need to manually gate the switch with a trait-based condition and ensure that trait is updated when the valve fires. The State Machine centralizes the logic: one transition, one On State, and every downstream Spark reacts to it.

---

## Worked example: branching scenario outcome

A scenario presents two choices within a single Chapter, and the debrief at the end of that Chapter reflects which choice was made.

**Setup:** Place one State Machine (Named). States: "ChoiceA", "ChoiceB".

**Tree 1 — Choice A button:**
```
Interacted (button A) → Go to Named State (ChoiceA)
```

**Tree 2 — Choice B button:**
```
Interacted (button B) → Go to Named State (ChoiceB)
```

**Tree 3 — State Machine response:**
```
On State (ChoiceA) → Visible (feedback A, on) → Visible (feedback B, off)
On State (ChoiceB) → Visible (feedback B, on) → Visible (feedback A, off)
```

The State Machine tracks which choice was made and drives the correct feedback — all within the same Chapter.

**State Machine values do not persist across Chapter changes.** When the learner moves to a new Chapter, the State Machine resets to its default state. If you need to carry a value across Chapters — for example, routing a learner to a different debrief Chapter based on a choice made earlier — use a **Datum Spark** with Is Persistent enabled. The destination Chapter must contain a Datum Instance with the same instance name and Is Persistent also enabled.

---

## Things to know

**On State 0 fires at Chapter load.** The **On State** Cause wired to state 0 (or to the first named state in a Named State Machine) fires automatically when the Chapter starts, before any user interaction. This is intentional — use it to initialize anything that depends on the State Machine being in its default state.

**Setting the same state again has no effect.** If a **Go to State** Effect targets the state the State Machine is already in, the **On State** Cause does not fire. Nothing happens. If you need a repeated trigger, use a different Cause-Effect pattern rather than cycling back to the current state.

**A State Machine affects only what is wired to it.** A State Machine does not automatically lock or hide anything — it just fires its **On State** Cause when it transitions. All scene response to a state change must be explicitly wired.

---

## Reference

For full parameter details on all State Machine Causes and Effects:

- [State Machine](../../reference/config-sparks/state-machine/) — numeric states
- [State Machine (Named)](../../reference/config-sparks/state-machine-named/) — named states

title: Your First Behavior
content:
# Your First Behavior

This walkthrough takes you from an empty canvas to a working behavior in a few steps. By the end, clicking a cube in play mode will cause a sphere to pulse with a blue highlight.

## What you need

Place two Spark Instances in the scene before you start: a "Cube 1x1" and a "Sphere 1x1". Any two Entity Sparks will work, but these names are used throughout the steps below.

---

## Step 1: Select the Cube instance and open the Behaviors tab

Click the "Cube 1x1" instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer to select it. In the left panel, click the "Behaviors" tab. The canvas opens — it is empty because no behaviors have been wired yet.

You can also select an instance from the Entities tab in the Instances pane (lower right). Any selection method updates the Instance dropdown in the Behaviors tab. See [Behaviors tab](../ui-panels/behavior-panel.md#selecting-a-spark-instance) for the full list.

---

## Step 2: Add a Cause

At the top of the Behaviors tab, confirm the instance dropdown shows "Cube 1x1". Open the Causes dropdown and select "Interacted". Click the **+** button. An "Interacted" node appears on the canvas.

The "Interacted" Cause fires when the player activates the instance. In VR, this means pointing the laser pointer at the object and pressing the trigger. In Builder play mode, press **E** while close to and facing the object to simulate the interaction — you must be within approximately 1 meter or the interaction will not register. It has two outputs: left ("Interact On") and right ("Interact Off").

> **Prerequisite:** The "Interacted" Cause requires "Is Interactable" to be enabled on the cube instance. Open the "Traits" tab, find "Is Interactable", and turn it on. A yellow warning triangle on the node indicates the trait is missing.

---

## Step 3: Add an Effect — on a different instance

The Effect you want lives on the sphere, not the cube. Use the instance dropdown at the top of the Behaviors tab to switch to "Sphere 1x1". Open the Effects dropdown, select "Highlight", and click **+**. A "Highlight" node appears on the canvas.

The "Highlight" Effect adds a pulsing blue highlight to the sphere. It has an "Enabled" checkbox on the node that controls whether the highlight turns on or off. Leave it checked (on).

---

## Step 4: Wire the Cause to the Effect

Every node has connection dots: an output dot at the bottom and an input dot at the top. To wire:

1. Find the output dot at the bottom of the "Interacted" node (left output, "Interact On").
2. Click and drag from that dot toward the input dot at the top of the "Highlight" node.
3. Release when the wire snaps to the input dot. The wire connects automatically when dragged close enough.

You now have a behavior tree: the "Interacted" Cause on the cube drives the "Highlight" Effect on the sphere.

<!-- SCREENSHOT PLACEHOLDER: add a screenshot of the Behaviors canvas showing the Interacted node connected to the Highlight node -->

---

## Step 5: Test in play mode

Click the triangle (play) button in the bottom-right of the Map Explorer. The button turns purple when play mode is active. Behaviors do not run in edit mode — you must be in play mode to test them.

Face the cube and press **E** to activate it ("Interact On"). The sphere highlights blue. Press **E** again ("Interact Off") — the highlight turns off. (In VR, this is the laser pointer trigger. In Builder play mode, E is the keyboard equivalent.)

> **If pressing E does nothing:** confirm you are within approximately 1 meter of the cube. Builder play mode has a shorter interaction range than VR. Move closer and try again.

Click the stop button to return to edit mode.

---

## What you just built

This behavior tree spans two Spark Instances: a Cause on the cube wired to an Effect on the sphere. When the player interacts with the cube, the signal travels down the wire to the "Highlight" Effect and sets the sphere's highlight state to on. The "Interact Off" output is unwired, so releasing the interaction does nothing yet.

A few things worth noting:

- The behavior canvas is not limited to a single instance. You can wire Causes from any instance to Effects on any other instance.
- "Highlight" is a state-setter, not a toggle. The checked state means "highlight on." To turn it off on a separate trigger, you would add a second "Highlight" node with the checkbox unchecked and wire separately.
- Nothing runs in edit mode. If you activate the cube and nothing happens, confirm you are in play mode (purple button).
